title: How do Manchester City manage the Rodri dilemma?
summary: BBC Sport looks at what City's new-look midfield could be like and whether it is time to cash in on Rodri.
full_text:
How do Manchester City manage the Rodri dilemma?
- Published
Manchester City are in flux.
Replacing a manager after 10 years is no easy feat, let alone when there appears to be a squad overhaul too.
Four of the starters in City's Treble-winning side of 2022-23 - Manuel Akanji, Nathan Ake, Bernardo Silva and John Stones - have left this summer, with the Blues signing £116m Elliot Anderson and promising 17-year-old Jeremy Monga.
And the changes might not end there.
Fresh from captaining Spain to World Cup victory, Rodri will head for back surgery on Monday with just a year left on his contract, amid increasing speculation about his future.
It is not clear how long the 30-year-old will spend on the sidelines, but one thing new boss Enzo Maresca was clear on in his first news conference was that he wants to keep him.
But with reports that Real Madrid are "operating on the basis" of Rodri joining them,, external what do City do?
Will they look to cash in when Rodri returns to fitness, or keep to Maresca's stance?
And how might Maresca's midfield operate - with or without Rodri?
What's the background?
When Rodri returned from an anterior cruciate ligament injury last year, there will have been plenty who wondered whether he would return to the Ballon d'Or-winning levels he had reached at his peak.
Pep Guardiola - the man Maresca has replaced - said last October: "In the World Cup, he will be the best Rodri, and next season he will be the best Rodri."
Guardiola was proved right on the first count. Not only did Rodri captain Spain to World Cup success but he was also awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.
Maresca was unequivocal when asked for his view on Friday.
"I think every manager wants to have Rodri because he is a top player," he said.
"But now, surgery on Monday... he needs a holiday... he needs to rest and recover and then he will be back with us."
The plan seems clear, therefore - look to retain one of the best players in world football rather than sell him.
But there will have to be contingencies in place.
One of these will be the presence of Anderson, while City are monitoring 18-year-old Lille midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi, who impressed for Morocco in the World Cup.
What does a Maresca midfield look like?
To understand how Rodri, Anderson and someone like Bouaddi might come together, it is key to understand Maresca's game model.
As a disciple of positional play, he draws comparisons between his football and chess.
"There are a lot of similarities," Maresca said. "The most important is positional play and strategy.
"For a coach, it's important to have the mentality of a chess player: develop a plan, study counter-moves, choose the arrangement of the pieces."
Maresca's strategy has largely been rooted in an on-the-ball shape that looks like a 3-2-2-3.
One of Rodri's most useful qualities in a Maresca side would be his ability to move between these predefined positions on the pitch.
Throughout the World Cup, for example, we saw him drop into the backline when former City team-mate Aymeric Laporte pushed up with the ball.
Naturally, Rodri spent most of the game in a holding midfield position, but when space opened up he was more than capable of pushing forward too.
1 of 3
At their best, Maresca's sides use rotations of players within the 3-2-2-3. His innovation often comes in the form of creating this shape in new ways.
Defending as a 4-4-2 before attacking in the 3-2-2-3, it was Stones who stepped up from centre-back into a midfield pair with Rodri during City's Treble-winning season, when Maresca was assistant manager.
At Chelsea, one of Maresca's more unique tweaks involved playing Moises Caicedo at right-back. Defending with a back four before again attacking in a 3-2-2-3 shape, Caicedo would move from right-back into one of the holding midfield positions.
Where does Anderson fit in?
Here is where the signing of Anderson makes such sense.
Throughout his career, the 23-year-old has played in every midfield and attacking position at one point. For England, he has frequently dropped into defence to form a back five out of possession.
Alongside Rodri, Anderson would be able to sit deep, allowing the Spaniard to showcase his attacking quality - and vice versa.
Both players would be capable of taking turns in dropping deeper to maintain the balance of the team if strong carriers of the ball like Marc Guehi or Josko Gvardiol were to push forward.
Piggy-backing on the success of Rodri's work with Bernardo Silva, City would hope their new versatile and combative winger-turned-holding-midfielder will bring about similar success.
Bouaddi - like Anderson - has played in a number of roles, more specifically holding midfield, right-back and centre-back.
His ability to occupy those positions - with strong defending and elegance on the ball - replicates some of the work Stones did for City.
The club are looking at young and intelligent footballers capable of playing for possession-heavy sides. More important, however, is their ability to be positionally versatile across the roles Maresca's system demands.
When numerous players can move into any of the positions that open up, it can result in a structured yet fluid team that become harder for the opposition to defend against – think Luis Enrique's Paris St-Germain.
But this takes both time and tutelage.
What if Rodri goes?
City will look better with Rodri, who possesses an understanding of positioning, speed and risk that Anderson and future signings may take time to grasp.
After all, it took Rodri a few seasons to navigate the change in environment under Fernandinho's wing.
But should he go, Maresca has previously shown an impressive ability to recognise positions players could move into but haven't yet done: Stones into holding midfield, Caicedo into full-back, Marc Cucurella into attacking midfield... the list goes on.
Whether or not City further bolster their squad, Maresca will hope to have a greater number of pieces to place on his board - a departure from Guardiola's approach of maintaining a smaller squad.
That factor - and this holds true whether or not Rodri stays - should give City's new boss a greater chance of landing on a working formula next season.

title: How Volker Turk won a new term as UN rights chief despite Israel opposition
summary: UN General Assembly votes 144-10 to grant Turk a new four-year term, despite objections from the US, Israel and Russia.
full_text:
How Volker Turk won a new term as UN rights chief despite Israel opposition
The UN General Assembly voted 144-10 to grant Turk a new four-year term, despite objections from the US, Israel and Russia.
Volker Turk has been elected as United Nations human rights chief for another four-year term, despite strong objections from the United States, Russia and Israel.
The United Nations General Assembly vote on Friday means Turk, who has served in the role since 2022, will become the first person to serve two full terms as the UN rights chief since the position was created in 1993.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3ICC prosecutor Karim Khan removed over ‘political’ sex abuse claims
- list 2 of 3Knesset dissolves: How will Israel vote in October’s general election?
- list 3 of 3At least 21 killed as Ukraine and Russia continue to trade attacks
Who is Turk and why has his reappointment caused controversy?
Who is Volker Turk?
Turk, an Austrian lawyer, joined the United Nations in 1999 and went on to work in the organisation’s refugee agency. This included posts in Malaysia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
He later worked in senior roles at UN headquarters in New York, including as assistant secretary-general for strategic coordination under UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. The two are believed to have a close relationship.
In his role as UN rights chief, Turk has been highly critical of both Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. He has also been vocal on conflicts and rights abuses in Afghanistan, Sudan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nicaragua.
How was he reappointed?
The UN General Assembly overwhelmingly backed a proposal by Guterres to give Turk another four-year term with 144 votes in favour, 10 against and 13 abstentions.
Earlier, the assembly shot down a US proposal to delay the vote until the end of next week as well as a Russian bid to extend Turk’s term until the end of the year only.
How has Turk angered the US, Russia and Israel?
The role of UN human rights chief is inherently controversial because it requires public criticism of governments of UN members for alleged rights violations.
Turk’s outspoken criticism of policies in Israel, Russia and the US has put him at odds with all three countries.
Turk has repeatedly criticised Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, its deadly assault on Lebanon, and a “shameful” lack of accountability for its rights abuses in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Turk has also described Russia’s war in Ukraine as “senseless” and a “blatant affront to the UN Charter and the whole body of international law”.
On the US, he has raised concerns about the war on Iran and the “dehumanisation” of immigrants under President Donald Trump, citing routine “abuse and denigration of migrants and refugees”.
Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs criticised Turk’s record, saying that under his leadership the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights has “erased the atrocities of October 7, misused funds, and betrayed UN neutrality in favor of corrupt political radicalism”.
Russia’s Deputy Ambassador to the UN Dmitry Chumakov accused Turk of bias and making unfounded allegations against Russia.
What objections were raised to Turk’s reappointment?
Guterres, whose own term is due to end at the end of this year, has faced criticism for how he managed the reappointment. Critics say the vote was rushed and the selection of a rights chief should have been left to his successor.
The UN secretary-general, whose term expires in December, sent letters to regional groups at the UN earlier this month informing them of his intention to reappoint Turk, and held the vote just weeks later.
The US Department of State criticised the vote for being rushed and said it was “another example of the UN’s inherent corruption and incompetence”.
The US also accused Turk of turning “a blind eye to real atrocities and instead pursued a radical ideological agenda”. US Deputy Ambassador Jeff Bartos claimed before Friday’s vote that reappointing Turk would prove that the General Assembly “is dysfunctional”.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry called Guterres’s push for a second term for Turk a “moral failure,” saying that the choice should be left to his successor.
UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said Guterres had followed UN rules and engaged “in a very transparent manner” in appointing Turk, including by holding prior consultations with member states and regional groups.
What other criticism has Turk faced?
Turk’s critics say he could have done more to publicly follow up on a report issued by his predecessor, former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, that said China’s detention of Uighurs and other mostly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang may amount to crimes against humanity.
Turk also has stopped short of joining independent UN rights experts who have accused Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Turk’s office said he had used both private engagement with Beijing and his public advocacy to support human rights in China.

title: Israel arrests dozens of Palestinians in West Bank amid settler attacks
summary: Military crackdown follows a shooting that killed four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers.
full_text:
Israel arrests dozens of Palestinians in West Bank amid settler attacks
Military crackdown follows a shooting that killed four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers.
Israel is pushing ahead with its military crackdown across the occupied West Bank, arresting dozens following a shooting that killed four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers.
On Saturday morning, Israeli forces arrested nearly 50 Palestinians in the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus, where Friday’s shooting took place, while raiding roughly 70 homes.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Israel launches clampdown after deadly violence in occupied West Bank
- list 2 of 4Funerals held for four Palestinians killed in deadly West Bank shooting
- list 3 of 4Netanyahu to meet Trump at White House next week amid Iran war escalation
- list 4 of 4Israel’s illegal settlements are Europe’s credibility test
Footage posted by Quds News Network shows two blindfolded men being led away by Israeli soldiers. The arrests are part of what Israel’s military has described as an “extensive” operation launched in response to Friday’s shooting.
On Friday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz ordered a “wide-scale military operation” in Palestinian villages across the occupied West Bank following an attack near the illegal Havat Gilad settlement that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others.
According to sources and witnesses, Israeli settlers attacked several Palestinian communities in the Nablus governorate, setting fire to Palestinian homes and other property.
The Palestinian Health Ministry says at least 87 Palestinians have been killed by Israelis in attacks across the West Bank since the beginning of the year, 21 of them by settlers, who critics say have become emboldened by the lack of international pressure on Israel to end its siege of Gaza, as well as the rhetoric of far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Albanese calls attacks as ‘pogroms’
UN Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese on Saturday described Israeli attacks against Palestinian civilians across the occupied West Bank as “pogroms,” calling for an immediate arms embargo and a halt to trade with Israel.
“Pogroms against defenseless civilians all over the West Bank, while Gaza is under fire,” Albanese posted on X.
She accused Israeli civilians and the army of “joining forces” in the attacks, arguing that responsibility was not limited to Netanyahu or “a few rotten apples”.
“Arms embargo now — stop trade now,” Albanese said, adding that such measures are required under international law.
Israeli human rights groups have also urged the international community to take immediate action to stop state-backed settler violence in the West Bank, which has surged since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in 2023.
In the West Bank, several arrests were also made in the northern city of Jenin, as well as in towns and villages across the governorate. Israeli forces raided multiple homes and deployed large numbers of troops.
Elsewhere, Israeli forces raided Tubas in the northeast and the Far’a refugee camp south of the city.
Soldiers arrived in Tubas in a large convoy of military vehicles and were deployed across several neighbourhoods, raiding homes for about three hours, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. They then headed to the Far’a refugee camp.
Israeli forces also raided several other locations, including the village of Far’ata, east of Qalqilya, where at least eight Palestinians were injured, according to Al Mayadeen English. The Aqbat Jabr refugee camp in Jericho and the village of Kobar in the Ramallah and el-Bireh Governorate were also among the locations targeted.
Funerals were held overnight for the four Palestinians killed in Tal on Friday.
Residents said they were forced to hold the funerals at night because Israeli authorities barred them from doing so during the day. According to reports, only a limited number of Palestinians were allowed to attend.
‘Happening all across the West Bank’
The shooting in Tal was the deadliest there in months, with both sides disputing what happened. Israelis are not permitted to enter Tal, which is under the control of the Palestinian Authority.
Footage shows rifle-wielding settlers confronting a crowd of Palestinians. Another video shows a Palestinian man seizing a gun from a settler before fatally shooting him in what appears to be self-defence. Israeli soldiers then shot and killed the Palestinian. Three other Palestinians were also killed.
Ubai Al Aboudi, a rights activist in Ramallah, told Al Jazeera that settler attacks on Palestinian villages are systemic and carried out with complete impunity, describing them as “not isolated incidents” but something “happening all across the West Bank”.
He pointed to an attack on the village of Tal on Friday, noting that it had also been targeted a week earlier on July 18.
“So-called hikers, as the Israeli officials called them, came into the village, burned a family house with the family still inside it, and it was a miracle that the residents of Tal were able to get that family out of the house before they were burned alive,” Al Aboudi said.
Human Rights Watch has also called on the Israeli government to take immediate action to prevent settlers from carrying out revenge attacks against Palestinians.
“The Israeli government didn’t prevent the settler attacks on Tal village, so now it needs to stop settler reprisals and escalating military action that will make a bad situation worse,” said Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“Years of lawlessness and impunity for attacks have turned the West Bank into a powder keg waiting to explode, and decisive action is urgently needed.”

title: India’s education minister resigns after weeks of ‘Cockroach’ protests
summary: Dharmendra Pradhan quits in first major concession from PM Narendra Modi's government after nationwide demonstrations.
full_text:
India’s education minister resigns after weeks of ‘Cockroach’ protests
Dharmendra Pradhan quits in first major concession from PM Narendra Modi’s government after nationwide demonstrations over exam paper leaks.
India’s Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned, handing a big victory to youth protesters nationwide who had demanded that he quit to take responsibility for a series of examination paper leaks.
Pradhan announced his resignation on X on Saturday, just as police fired tear gas to scatter the protesters in New Delhi, hours before their leaders were set to hold another round of talks with federal ministers.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Indian student protests: What’s next after Modi’s promise on exam leaks?
- list 2 of 4India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders hold talks with gov’t as protests continue
- list 3 of 4Indian activist Wangchuk ends 26-day hunger strike over exam paper leaks
- list 4 of 4‘Televising our revolution’: India’s Gen Z flips Modi’s social media game
“Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and across the country, so that antinational forces do not take advantage of this situation … I have sent my resignation letter to Prime Minister [Narendra Modi],” Pradhan wrote in his post.
“I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of the country’s youth.”
Pradhan said he did not want to allow tens of thousands of students calling for his resignation to be taken advantage of by “anti-national forces”.
He said he did not want to see pupils become “entangled in legal complexities” instead of studying and building their careers.
‘Democracy won!’
“We have done it,” said Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the satire movement that led the protests, to loud cheers at the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi, where authorities restricted access to the internet and closed 18 metro stations around it. Similar celebrations were also reported from other cities across the country.
In a post on X, the CJP said: “Cockroaches won… Democracy won!”
The CJP said it has three more demands: one crore rupees ($103,554) to the families of all students who died by suicide, no punitive action against people who participated in the protests, and a public apology from Delhi Police and the Rapid Action Force paramilitary over the attacks on the protesters.
In a post on X, the movement said the three demands are still “pending”.
“We won’t go like this,” founder Dipke said. “Remember, do not mess with cockroach.”
Anger has boiled over since police on Monday injured many students, launching baton charges and firing tear gas and even alleged pellet guns to deter crowds of protesters marching on parliament.
A second round of talks between senior members of the group and the government was due to take place on Saturday. It is not clear if that meeting will still go ahead. Talks were also held on Friday.
Modi’s government had earlier sought to ease tensions by announcing fast-track courts for cases involving exam paper leaks and saying it would introduce legislation to strengthen measures against cheating and corruption in the examination system.
The protests, one of the most visible signs of public dissent against Modi’s government in recent years, reflected growing anger over job scarcity, corruption and government accountability.

Zhu Kewei, China’s ambassador to the...
full_text:
How China is using film diplomacy to project a better image across Africa
From Burundi to Kenya to Morocco, film screenings, co-productions and cultural exchanges are helping to shape a new frontier of influence
The Chinese embassy in Bujumbura, the economic capital of Burundi, said the July 15 event offered “a beautiful example of cultural exchanges between the two countries” and that both sides were determined to “make cinema a vehicle for Sino-Burundian friendship”.
Zhu Kewei, China’s ambassador to the East African country, called cinema “a force capable of bridging language barriers, borders and cultures”, adding that “film carries a nation’s historical memories, cultural traditions, values and the emotions of its people”.
In addition to the film screenings, China and Burundi plan to expand cooperation through creator exchanges, artist mobility, university partnerships, co-productions and skills transfer.
As part of the China-Africa Year of Human and Cultural Exchanges, the festival in Burundi lined up seven Chinese films, including The Wandering Earth II, Changan and The Snow Leopard.

title: What a helicopter’s flight in the Taiwan Strait says about Beijing’s war plans
summary:
A People’s Liberation Army helicopter’s unprecedented flight in the Taiwan Strait has raised concerns in Taipei that Beijing is rehearsing a new kind of operation for a potential cross-strait conflict.
Taiwan’s defence ministry said it detected four PLA aircraft, including a helicopter and an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), operating around the island on July 20 and the following morning.
The helicopter and drone crossed the median line and remained east of it for nearly 9.5 hours in the “R9”...
full_text:
What a helicopter’s flight in the Taiwan Strait says about Beijing’s war plans
PLA may be practising ‘reconnaissance and strike’, in which drones and helicopters work in tandem alongside rocket artillery
A People’s Liberation Army helicopter’s unprecedented flight in the Taiwan Strait has raised concerns in Taipei that Beijing is rehearsing a new kind of operation for a potential cross-strait conflict.
Taiwan’s defence ministry said it detected four PLA aircraft, including a helicopter and an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), operating around the island on July 20 and the following morning.
The helicopter and drone crossed the median line and remained east of it for nearly 9.5 hours in the “R9” area – which Taiwan has designated as restricted – the first publicly reported case of a PLA helicopter lingering there for an extended period.
The median line is an unofficial boundary in the Taiwan Strait that divides the self-ruled island and mainland China.
The ministry said it closely monitored the aircraft using joint intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance assets and responded appropriately.
Military analysts, however, said the flight might signal a new operational pattern.
“This should not be viewed as an isolated flight,” said Chieh Chung, a research fellow at the Association of Strategic Foresight, a Taipei-based military think tank.

title: What’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine?
summary:
After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner

Laura Loomer, the online Maga provocateur, has never worked in the White House or anywhere else in the government, but her sudden conversion to the Ukrainian cause this week is significant because her social media posts often have real policy implications in the second Trump administration.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Laura Loomer, the online Maga provocateur, has never worked in the White House or anywhere else in the government, but her sudden conversion to the Ukrainian cause this week is significant because her social media posts often have real policy implications in the second Trump administration.
The rightwing commentator has spent the last few days in Kyiv, where she announced a newfound sympathy for Ukraine in its long war with Russia, and admitted that she had previously fallen for Russian propaganda.
Loomer – who has previously echoed Kremlin talking points to her 2 million followers on social media – has enjoyed direct access to Trump since the 2024 presidential campaign. During the early months after Trump returned to office, Loomer used her online presence to push for ideological purges of government personnel, including many in the national security arena.
For a time, her power to break careers among foreign policy officials made her seem as if she were Trump’s de facto national security adviser.
It is unclear whether she still has that kind of pull inside the White House, but Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, certainly took her seriously when she arrived this week, holding a private meeting with her on Thursday.
Three days earlier, Loomer posted about experiencing her first air raid, as Russian missiles pounded the Ukrainian capital
“This is everyday for every Ukrainian,” she posting, adding she felt that she had been “an asshole for minimizing the struggle of Ukrainians for the last 5 years”.
“I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. There are people in Ukraine who have to run to a bomb shelter everyday and some of us had the audacity to say Russia wasn’t wrong because we believed the lie that Ukraine is a country full of Nazi sympathizers. We have been so propagandized by Russia and we don’t even realize it.”
Before their meeting on Thursday, Zelenskyy’s office posted a statement saying: “It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are.”
Loomer’s change of heart is potentially important not only because she is close to Trump, but also because she has long served as a reliable barometer of Maga attitudes.
Loomer has long been disdainful of Ukraine, adopting what could only be described as a pro-Russian perspective. Many in Maga circles have for years held positive views of the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, thanks to Russian propaganda that portrayed him as a bulwark against homosexuality and a defender of fundamentalist Christianity. They became convinced that the Russia-Ukraine war was a proxy fight between Russia’s fundamentalist Christianity and the EU’s western secularism.
Loomer’s shift comes at a critical moment for Ukraine, which recently lost one of its strongest supporters in Washington with the death this month of Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator from South Carolina who had consistently pushed for increased sanctions on Russia to punish Moscow for its invasion of Ukraine.
But Loomer’s change also coincides with what appears to be an important recent shift in Trump’s own views on Ukraine.
Trump returned to office openly hating Ukraine, at least in part because of the 2019 impeachment over his attempt to hold up aid to Ukraine in exchange for dirt on Joe Biden. Early in his second term, Trump humiliated Zelenskyy in an Oval Office meeting, cut off direct the supply of US weapons and forced Ukraine’s European allies to buy American weapons for Kyiv instead.
But Trump likes winners, and even without full support from Washington, Ukraine has been able to slow Russia’s advance. Kyiv has become a global leader in drone technology, and it has taken the war to Russia itself with long-range missile attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure, leading to an energy crisis in one of the world’s biggest oil-producing nations.
Clearly impressed with Ukraine’s performance, Trump announced at the Nato summit in Turkey earlier this month that the US would license Patriot missile technology to Ukraine, allowing Kyiv to produce the advanced air defense missiles on its own.
At the same time, Trump also supported a move in Congress, which had been backed by Graham, to impose new sanctions on Russia, while also seeming to back off an earlier insistence that Ukraine would have to agree to give up large swaths of territory in exchange for any US-brokered peace deal with Russia.
Trump’s policy shifts were modest, but significant; it is possible that Loomer changed her position simply in order to stay in lockstep with Trump.
But her about-face could be even more politically significant if it represents a broader thawing of Maga attitudes towards Ukraine and an awakening to the dangers of Russian propaganda.

title: What Octogenarian Pop Divas Show Us About a Life Well-Lived
summary: Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick, all in their 80s, show us that conviction outlasts fashion, writes Debbie Millman.
full_text:
On May 20, Cher turned 80 years old. Beyond a celebration of one spectacular career, her birthday is an occasion to consider what it means for a woman to maintain long-term relevance. It opens a larger question about endurance, public scrutiny, and what it takes to live a long, authentic life.
Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick, all now in their 80s, were criticized for qualities that made them distinctive: being too country, too Jewish, too outspoken, too ambitious, too artificial, too stubborn. Rather than soften those edges, they built careers around them. The traits that once made them targets of ridicule eventually became their signatures.
In a culture that prizes constant reinvention, these octogenarian pop divas suggest another path: longevity through self-definition. They evolved, certainly, but without surrendering the core identities that made them recognizable in the first place. A life well-lived, they remind us, is not the life that pleased the most people, made the fewest demands, or aged into quiet respectability. A good life is one lived on its own terms, refusing every invitation to become smaller, softer, or less fully oneself.
Cher has spent more than six decades in the public eye, moving through music, television, film, fashion, tabloid culture, political commentary, heartbreak, reinvention, ridicule, camp, glamour, and triumph. She’s won a Grammy, an Emmy, an Academy Award, three Golden Globes, and is the only artist to have a number one single on a Billboard chart in seven consecutive decades.
She has been labeled too artificial, too outrageous, too sexual, too blunt, and too much. In the 1970s, her collaboration with Bob Mackie produced dresses that seemed designed to violate every rule of respectable female presentation: sheer, beaded, feathered, midriff-baring, unapologetically theatrical. In 1975, she appeared on the cover of TIME magazine in what was referred to as designer Bob Mackie’s “naked dress,”and in 1986, after being passed over for an Oscar nomination for the movie Mask despite winning Best Actress at Cannes, she arrived at the Academy Awards in a black Mackie ensemble with a towering feathered headdress, a bare midriff, and enough defiance to overwhelm the room.
The criticism intensified when Cher refused to separate glamour from sexuality as she aged. In 1989, the video for “If I Could Turn Back Time,” filmed aboard the USS Missouri, placed her in a sheer black bodysuit, fishnets, leather jacket, and little else, performing for a cheering crowd of sailors. MTV initially banned the video and later aired it only after 9 p.m. The Navy, which had expected something more conservative, was reportedly embarrassed by the result. What the controversy revealed was not merely discomfort with a costume, but discomfort with a woman in her forties presenting herself as erotic, funny, commanding, and entirely in control of the spectacle.
Through all of it, she never seemed remotely interested in becoming more palatable. At one point in the late 1980s, her body was so scrutinized that there was a debate as to whether or not she had several ribs removed. (She didn’t.) Cher has acknowledged some cosmetic surgery, denied the more lurid inventions, refused the premise that her body required public adjudication, and defiantly stated, “If I want to put my tits on my back, it is nobody’s business but my own.”
Cher’s dexterity shows up beyond how she survived being mocked for excess. It is revealed by how she transformed excess into architecture. Her costumes, wigs, cosmetic surgery, her public romances, the one-name fame: they constitute the visual and emotional vocabulary she has deftly controlled. Spectacle has never been a mask Cher has hid behind; it is the medium through which she insists on being seen.
This refusal has become Cher’s version of authorship. She has never disappeared into the trope expected of aging women. Instead, she made “too much” the unmistakable, driving force of her power.
Dolly Parton, also 80, spent years being deemed too country, too buxom, too rhinestoned, too blonde, too much of an exaggeration to be taken seriously. Late-night hosts and interviewers repeatedly treated her body as public property and her appearance as a punchline. Johnny Carson joked about her breasts on The Tonight Show; countless others followed the same overly trodden path.
Parton’s genius was that rather than avoiding the joke, she took control of it. She understood, earlier than almost anyone, that being underestimated could become its own form of power.
Long before she was appreciated as a national treasure, Parton knew who was really in control of the performance. When she joked that, “it costs a lot of money to look this cheap,” she playfully named the labor, money, intelligence, and craft inside the caricature. Her blonde hair, acrylic nails, high heels, rhinestones, waist-cinching silhouettes, and curves were not accidents of taste. They were the materials of a persona she built deliberately, then protected ferociously.
Parton turned exaggeration into authorship through repetition and scale. On album covers like Jolene, she presented mountain-girl glamour as a code. In the film 9 to 5, she transformed the image of the underestimated secretary into a working woman with wit, strategy, and rage. At Dollywood, which opened under her name in 1986 near the Tennessee mountains where she was raised, she converted her story into infrastructure: a theme park, a regional employer, a monument to Appalachian storytelling, craft, music, and belonging. What might have been dismissed as kitsch became an economic and cultural engine, directly employing approximately 4,000 people, creating more than 23,000 jobs in the region, and contributing $1.8 billion in annual economic impact to Tennessee.
In the process, Parton became one of the most accomplished songwriters, performers, philanthropists, and entrepreneurs in the world. She has written thousands of songs, including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “9 to 5,” and “I Will Always Love You,” the latter becoming a rare song that defined two different eras through two different women’s voices. Parton has been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, the Country Music Hall of Fame, the Songwriters Hall of Fame, and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Her Imagination Library, founded in 1995 in honor of her father, who never learned to read or write, has now gifted more than 300 million books to children. The program began in her home county in Tennessee and has grown across multiple countries.
What makes Parton’s endurance so instructive is that she never abandoned the mountain-girl mythology from which she first emerged. She expanded it. She made it capacious enough to hold country music, film, children’s literacy, vaccine philanthropy, theme parks, baking mixes, fashion, and business. The rhinestones were never a distraction from the seriousness of her work. They were part of the strategy.
The starmaker machinery has long depended on a narrow definition of beauty and controlling the behavior of women. Barbra Streisand, now 84, was told early and often that the things that made her unmistakable were liabilities. She was too Jewish, too nasal, too Brooklyn, too ambitious, too controlling, too unwilling to be remade into someone else’s idea of a star.
From the start of her career, people told her to fix her nose. In 1964, even this magazine reported as much. In her memoir, she recalls being told by several people that she should get a nose job and have her teeth capped. But she feared that changing her nose might change her voice, and refused, certain that her talent should be enough.
It was enough, but not before the culture made her pay for it. When Streisand fought to make Yentl, the 1983 film she co-wrote, produced, directed, and starred in, she spent years trying to persuade Hollywood that she could direct it. The film itself is about a Jewish woman who refuses th

title: Democratizing weather derivatives through tokenization could be crypto's most important real-world use case
full_text:
Democratizing weather derivatives through tokenization could be crypto's most important real-world use case
Main Street, which faces the most significant climate-related financial risk, currently lacks an avenue to hedge weather-related risks, argues CoinDesk’s Omkar Godbole.
- Weather-related disasters and climate transition risks are growing rapidly, yet the traditional weather derivatives market remains tiny, opaque and largely inaccessible to those most exposed.
- Tokenizing weather derivatives on public blockchains could automate payouts via smart contracts, reduce counterparty risk and open climate-risk hedging to farmers, small businesses and other non-institutional users.
- Early efforts to bring reliable meteorological data onchain, such as partnerships between weather data providers and blockchain networks, aim to solve the oracle problem and enable scalable, transparent weather finance products.
“Since the 1980s the number of registered weather-related loss events tripled, and the inflation-adjusted losses have increased fivefold. These trends are set to continue and could threaten assets worth 20 per cent of global GDP."
That's Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney talking about climate risks in his 2021 book Value(s): Building a Better World for All.
I recently finished reading this 600-page book and it has been an eye opener on many levels, especially on weather, a space I last tracked at my gig on a currencies and commodities research desk in Mumbai from 2012 to 2014. Part of my job involved tracking natural gas prices, which take cues from weather forecasts and sometimes weather derivatives, more specifically options on heating degree days (HDD) and cooling degree days (CDD).
Back then, it struck me how broken, fragmented and little known these weather options were, leaving the bulk of the world’s population exposed to the financial devastation of weather and climate risks (not to mention the physical risks).
Omkar Godbole is a co-managing editor on CoinDesk’s Markets team.
Now, after spending a decade in crypto, I believe the most important real-world use case of tokenization, blockchain and smart contracts could be tokenizing weather derivatives and not merely creating a digital warehouse of traditional yield-generating assets such as bonds.
Let me explain why.
Weather derivatives are financial instruments that pay out when specific climate conditions cross predetermined thresholds. For example, a utility company might buy a contract that pays if winter temperatures stay unusually warm, cutting heating demand and revenue. An airline might hedge against the cost of flight cancellations caused by storms. A farmer in India might protect against a failed monsoon.
These instruments exist precisely because weather is one of the largest unhedged financial risks in the global economy. According to estimates by the World Meteorological Organization, weather-related disasters have caused a global economic loss of over $2 trillion in the past decade alone.
The traditional weather derivatives market is broken
The problem is that the market built to manage this risk is itself broken.
Weather derivatives are highly specific, mostly bespoke contracts based on localized risks and are frequently short term, which severely curtails secondary trading activity. The entire market has a notional value of roughly $25 billion, a rounding error compared to interest rate or credit derivatives markets, and an equally striking rounding error relative to the $2 trillion in weather-related losses recorded over the past decade — let alone the scale of potential disasters ahead.
It is also worth noting that weather-related financial risk is not limited to the destruction caused by extreme events. Carney calls these physical risks.
There are equally significant transition risks. As the global economy moves toward a lower-carbon economy, Carney argues, changes in policies and technologies could trigger billions in losses from stranded assets — those that no longer comply with new regulatory frameworks or emerging technologies, and therefore no longer hold the value they once did.
The current weather derivatives market is simply not equipped to handle either risk adequately. The market that exists today is a fragmented, bespoke market riddled with limited contract standardization, weak pricing transparency and significant counterparty risk. It is dominated by large institutions such as energy utilities firms, which account for about 40% of all contracts, followed by agriculture at 25%. The people most exposed to weather risk, like smallholder farmers, small logistics operators, micro-businesses in climate-vulnerable emerging markets, have no access to these instruments. The market is too small, too illiquid and too opaque for anyone without a Bloomberg terminal and an institutional balance sheet to track and navigate.
In other words, Main Street, which faces the most significant climate-related financial risk, is effectively left without an avenue to hedge risks. The very market designed to help the world manage climate risk is failing at the job, and the failure is structural rather than technical.
Democratizing weather derivatives with tokenization
This is where tokenization enters, and where I think the crypto industry has a genuinely important role to play in democratizing weather risk hedging. It’s an initiative that I think is significantly more important than simply offering traditional yield-generating assets like bonds onchain.
The core advantages of putting weather derivatives on a blockchain are not theoretical. Smart contracts can automatically trigger payouts when verified weather data crosses a predetermined threshold, while bypassing manual processing, disputes, delays, and counterparty risk. With tokenized weather derivatives, a farmer in a rain-dependent economy no longer needs a Goldman Sachs relationship to hedge against a failed monsoon. A parametric insurance product built on a smart contract that reads verified rainfall data and pays out automatically is, in principle, exactly the kind of market that properly prices and distributes climate risk.
In Value(s), Carney puts it well: "We need financial markets to work alongside climate policies in order to maximize their impact. With the right foundations, the financial system can build a virtuous circle of better understanding of tomorrow's risks, better pricing for investors, better decisions by policymakers and a smoother transition to a lower-carbon economy."
Tokenization also addresses the liquidity and accessibility problems that have stunted the traditional market. Fractional ownership allows weather risk to be divided into smaller units.and the resulting composability facilitates integration of weather derivatives with lending protocols, insurance products and yield-generating instruments. Transparency on every trade, every position, every settlement recorded on a public blockchain addresses the opacity that has historically made price discovery poor and participation limited.
Tokenized weather derivatives will only work if the data feeding them is reliable. That brings us to the oracle problem – that is, getting tamper-proof, real-time weather data onto a blockchain in a form smart contracts can trust. And it is being addressed by some companies already.
Kweather, a leading South Korean weather big data platform, and Flare, a data-centric blockchain network, recently signed a letter of intent to bring meteorological datasets, including temperature, rainfall and other climate variables, onchain. They aim to enable weather finance products for DeFi, parametric insurance and climate risk markets. This initiative is still very early; it is a pilot, and a letter of intent is not a working product.
Tokenization won't fix climate change. But it might fix the market that was supposed to help us manage it. In a world where weather risk is only going to grow, that is no small thing.

title: North Korea arrests bank hacking ring tied to crypto laundering: Report
summary: Daily NK reported that North Korea arrested former state cyber operators accused of hacking two state banks and laundering funds through crypto.
full_text:
North Korea arrests bank hacking ring tied to crypto laundering: Report
Daily NK reported that North Korea arrested former state cyber operators accused of hacking two state banks and laundering funds through crypto.
North Korean authorities have reportedly arrested a group of former state cyber operators and IT specialists accused of hacking two state banks and laundering stolen funds through cryptocurrency.
South Korean outlet Daily NK reported Thursday, citing an anonymous source in Pyongyang, that the group allegedly hacked the internal networks of North Korea’s central bank and the Foreign Trade Bank, converting stolen state funds into cryptocurrency before laundering them through China-based brokers.
Cointelegraph could not independently verify the report.
If confirmed, the reported arrests would mark a rare case of North Korean cyber operators being accused of stealing from their own government’s financial institutions.
Pyongyang is widely accused of directing state-backed hacking groups to steal from crypto companies to generate revenue and circumvent international sanctions.
Daily NK is a Seoul-based specialist news outlet that relies on a network of sources inside North Korea. Reporting from North Korea is difficult to verify independently because of the country’s restrictions on access and information.

title: Fidelity joins push for Senate passage of CLARITY Act
summary: Fidelity called on the US Senate to pass the CLARITY Act, joining industry groups and crypto firms pushing for market structure legislation.
full_text:
Fidelity joins push for Senate passage of CLARITY Act
Fidelity called on the US Senate to pass the CLARITY Act, joining industry groups and crypto firms pushing for market structure legislation.
Fidelity called on the US Senate to pass the CLARITY Act on Friday, saying clear digital asset regulations are needed to strengthen investor confidence, provide certainty for market participants and reinforce US leadership in global crypto markets.
The company joins a growing coalition of financial firms and crypto organizations urging US lawmakers to advance digital asset market structure legislation.
Earlier Friday, the Crypto Council for Innovation, the Digital Chamber and the Blockchain Association called on Senate leaders to bring the bill to the floor. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong also called for a full Senate floor vote on Wednesday.
The CLARITY Act would establish a regulatory framework for digital assets in the US. The bill needs 60 votes to pass the Senate, where Republicans hold a 52-47 majority. Republicans released updated bill text on Wednesday, but some Democrats argued the ethics provisions do not go far enough to address corruption concerns.
Fidelity is ranked as the world’s third-largest asset manager by the Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute. It reported $7.1 trillion in managed assets in its 2025 annual report.
Related: Here’s why the CLARITY Act’s ethics deal may be so hard to reach

title: Logistics giants are racing to keep up with healthcare boom as GLP-1s highlight need for cold storage
summary: Shipping and logistics companies are tapping into the growing market of healthcare as cold chain and temperature-controlled facilities become more crucial.
full_text:
As demand rises for specialized medications like GLP-1s, logistics companies including UPS and FedEx are adapting their strategies to be able to better ship and store those pharmaceuticals.
Most injectable GLP-1 medications, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, require refrigerated storage for shipment.
The Covid pandemic put healthcare logistics at center stage in 2020, as the shipping of temperature-controlled vaccines quickly became a crucial part of keeping the virus at bay. And as more money has been poured into new pharmaceutical innovations, the transportation of those products have come under the spotlight.
Logistics companies are now investing millions of dollars and strengthening dozens of temperature-controlled facilities to tap into the market.
In June, UPS announced a new $48 million investment in temperature-controlled facilities as it sees a growing demand for critical treatments. According to Growth Market Reports, the demand for temperature-sensitive biologics is projected to grow at an 8.3% compound annual growth rate through 2033 and reach a market value of roughly $39.1 billion.
Obesity and diabetes drugs, meanwhile, have been booming in popularity. A July Gallup poll found that 11% of Americans take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes in 2026, up from just 3% in 2024.
But if they're not stored and shipped at the correct temperature, they risk losing their efficacy.
The Food and Drug Administration has warned that improper storage during shipping can affect the medicine's quality and recommends patients do not use GLP-1 drugs that arrive "warm or with insufficient refrigeration."
Other biologics, like some vaccines, insulin and antibiotics, also require specialized shipment to maintain efficacy. For logistics companies, that means ensuring the proper storage and movement every step of the way.
Bulking up
Healthcare logistics have proven to be one of UPS' biggest opportunities. On an earnings call with analysts in April, CEO Carol Tomé said the company's global healthcare portfolio has gained market share every year since 2021, generating its first ever $3 billion healthcare revenue quarter in the first quarter of this year.
UPS President of Healthcare John Bolla told CNBC that the company is seeing more healthcare companies looking for partners to keep up with the volume.
"One of the biggest opportunities we see is supporting the shift toward more specialized therapies and more care delivered outside of traditional healthcare settings," Bolla said.
He said UPS is experiencing "rapid growth" in biologics, cell and gene therapies, though the biggest challenge is that the margin for error is small — even a brief stray from the correct temperature can ruin the medicines, Bolla said.
"But that's also what's creating such a significant opportunity in healthcare logistics," he said. "As treatments become more specialized and supply chains become more complex, healthcare companies need partners that can provide not just temperature-controlled storage or transportation, but end-to-end visibility, control and reliability across the entire network."
FedEx is also tapping into the trend, launching a life sciences organization earlier this month specifically to support the movement of pharmaceuticals and other healthcare products.
On an earnings call in June, FedEx's Chief Customer Officer Brie Carere told analysts that healthcare transportation revenue in fiscal year 2026 reached nearly $10 billion.
"We're building end-to-end solutions focused on global pharma customers, and what's so important with global pharma is that you have to recognize that there's a patient at the end of every delivery or someone that's waiting to be treated," said Nick Gennari, FedEx's president of healthcare. "So we take this very, very seriously."
With GLP-1s specifically, Gennari said there's an increasing complexity to delivering those medications, with forms ranging from injectables to oral pills and going direct-to-consumer. But with that complexity comes a growth opportunity for FedEx, which he said is "ideally positioned."
Gennari said FedEx has specialized technology, including its machine learning engine that allows customers to see product movement with predictive abilities, as well as its technology that identifies healthcare products and treats each differently depending on its unique needs.
Gennari also said he's "very comfortable" with the company's base capabilities and its plans for expansion, including cold-chain logistics.
"Much of the infrastructure that's required to be successful in this space, we already have. We have the airline; we have an incredible schedule; we have the lift capabilities. The network is hardened and works very well," he said.
Complex supply chains
C.H. Robinson told CNBC the logistics company had surpassed $1 billion in revenue in healthcare logistics alone over the past year, largely due to the growth in GLP-1 drugs, as it has been investing in temperature-controlled facilities.
"You need to really have that end-to-end connectivity, so you've got to have a really nice network and infrastructure built out in order to properly service the healthcare customers," said Ronnie Davis, the company's vice president of North American surface transportation.
Davis said the supply chain for medications has also become more complicated. In addition to requiring refrigeration, many drugs have a short shelf life and need to be delivered in precise windows of time.
"A lot of the innovation has been on getting the drugs to the market," Davis said. "I think what you're starting to see is that's really putting stress on the capabilities of the cold chain supply chains in the marketplace. … With the rise of GLP-1s and other specialized medicine, it's really creating a competitive nature for the same refrigerated supply resources that are there and, quite candidly, that supply is not unlimited, it's constrained."
Davis said C.H. Robinson is working to amp up its capabilities, especially to keep up with the higher volume. At the same time, he added, pharma companies are also trying to get creative to bring their products to market with a longer shelf life.
That innovation is also intersecting with the growth of artificial intelligence capabilities, according to Hendrik Venter, CEO of DHL Supply Chain. The logistics company uses AI to monitor critical life science products, tracking temperatures and anticipating where an issue might happen.
"You're seeing the industry moving from conventional to biopharma," Venter told CNBC. "You need to have a supply chain that is resilient and capable of shipping in all of these various temperature zones."
The company announced last year that it plans to invest 2 billion euros ($2.25 billion) in health logistics by 2030, with half of that allocated to the Americas.
A lot of pharmaceutical companies are also outsourcing their warehousing activities to DHL, Venter said. The company takes over those facilities, manages them and integrates them into the rest of their network.
DHL launched a pharmaceutical air corridor around the world, with a dedicated aircraft and connected network that ensures the drugs are not being shipped through separate regulatory environments.
"You cannot lose a shipment. You cannot replace it. It needs to be delivered on time, every time, in the right quality and temperatures," Venter said. "So we continue to selectively look at how to strengthen that network."

title: One fallen power line exposed a growing AI data center problem. Here’s how to fix it.
summary: A close call in Northern Virginia revealed just how poorly data centers respond to grid disruptions. Here's how to fix the problem.
full_text:
A power line went down outside of Washington, DC, this week. Normally, the grid would only need a few seconds to recover from such an event. But this one took more than 10 minutes because more than 3 gigawatts of data centers stopped drawing power nearly simultaneously.
The event caused voltage across the PJM grid to spike from Northern Virginia to Chicago, according to data collected by Ting Labs, a startup that runs an IoT sensor network out of people’s electrical sockets.
The event didn’t cause a blackout, but it did cause lights across the region to flicker. The incident demonstrated the effect that data centers can have on the grid — an outcome that experts believe will become more frequent.
Northern Virginia, which is in PJM’s territory, is home to the highest concentration of data centers in the world.
“It’s the canary in the coal mine,” Ricardo de Azevedo, CTO at ON.Energy, told TechCrunch. These sorts of events involving large loads like data centers are “happening more and more,” he added.
The event echoes one that happened two years ago, also on PJM’s grid, and it could foreshadow larger events if data centers aren’t built to more elegantly handle disruptions to power supplies. The PJM Interconnection manages grids from New Jersey to Illinois and serves 67 million customers, making it the largest grid operator in the United States.
When the power line went down this week, it triggered data centers to switch to backup power, and about 3.1 gigawatts of load vanished in about 30 seconds, according to PJM data. The grid appeared to recover somewhat, but a short time later additional loads dropped off. At its peak, PJM’s grid had an extra 3.49 gigawatts of electricity on it. It took another 11 minutes before it stabilized. The disconnected data centers represented around 3% of total demand on PJM at the time, according to Reuters.
A few percent may not sound like much, but the electrical grid needs to operate in a state of near-perfect balance, with supply and demand closely matched. If they don’t, voltages can sag or spike. The grid and devices connected to it can tolerate small fluctuations, but if those fluctuations grow too large, they’ll trigger failsafes within the grid or within individual facilities, causing them to disconnect.
When data centers in Northern Virginia sensed the fluctuation caused by the failed power line, they switched to backup power, which removed their load from the grid. As more data centers made the switch, they removed greater amounts of load from the grid. What started as a relatively small drop in supply became an even larger drop in demand, sending supply surging and causing light bulbs to flicker.
Most data centers make decisions in a split second, and those that disconnected this week appear to be no different. When the voltage dip reached them, they all decided to disconnect within a few seconds of each other, Ali Zain Banatwala, senior market models specialist at the Independent Electricity System Operator, told TechCrunch.
“We need to figure a way for these loads that are located next to each other to sequentially either disconnect or reconnect,” he said. A more orderly process would allow grid operators to develop more robust procedures in advance.
Alternatively, data centers could be built to absorb disruptions and not turn their backs to them. One startup, ON.Energy, has been working on a product to help data centers — and the grid — ride through events like the one that occurred this week.
The company has developed an uninterruptible power supply for an entire data center campus, covering not just servers but also chillers and other equipment. The company essentially hides the data center behind a bank of batteries connected to sophisticated power conversion equipment. All the grid “sees” is one consistent, well-behaved load rather than the peaks and valleys from each individual part of the data center. ON.Energy’s system allows data centers to ramp computing workloads up and down, including AI training, without bothering the grid.
Perhaps more important, it also means that data centers can absorb power fluctuations from the grid. Rather than disconnecting from the grid, ON.Energy’s system can use any extra power to charge its batteries, and if the flow dips, the system can dispatch power to servers. Plus, it can follow the grid’s lead within milliseconds, preventing sags or surges like the ones that caused this week’s problem for PJM.
ON.Energy is currently installing a total of 3 gigawatts worth of its systems at four different data center campuses, de Azevedo said.
Grid managers have also woken up to the problem.
ERCOT, for example, is going to require large loads like data centers to “ride through” disruptions, de Azevedo said.
The clock is ticking, though. The mass disconnection this week was twice as large as a similar event in 2024, when 60 data centers simultaneously disconnected, pulling 1.5 gigawatts of load from the grid. Back then, data centers accounted for about 6% of PJM’s load, according to Synapse Energy Economics. By 2040, they are expected to make up 24%. If the problem isn’t addressed soon, things could get a lot worse.

title: With help from data, art museums are reframing the visitor experience
summary: Museums are embracing data-driven curation and a shifting technology landscape.
full_text:
Giovanni Kanter goes to at least one art museum whenever he visits a new city. That’s on top of his regular exploration of galleries in New York, where the 25-year-old ICU nurse lives and studies. He typically discovers new artists and gallery openings through word of mouth, though he has recently started curating his social media feed to serve relevant content (he’s currently in what he terms a “surrealism phase”).
He was raised on visual art; he’s the son of painter Marianne Gargour and nephew of mixed-media artist Heather Hutchison and painter-printmaker Mark Thomas Kanter. His “exposure-oriented education” featured childhood visits to galleries and shows in and around Dallas, where he grew up, and in France, where he spent time with his grandparents.
But Kanter is an exception. Many other young people have a less immersive artistic education, perhaps shaped by occasional school trips or family visits to museums. If they haven’t internalized an instinct for what Kanter calls “moving through the art and absorbing it,” the museum experience is central to how they learn about and understand art.
Museums take this educational role seriously, and many institutions understand the need to sustain and broaden their appeal. “They used to be these big ivory towers of knowledge and history and thought and art,” said Hilary Knight, director of Change& in London and former director of digital at Tate. “Museums themselves are changing their role to be centers for discussion and encounter and to be much more participatory.”
To aid this transition, museums and other cultural institutions are increasingly using data to inform decisions about how to present the works they house. Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum (VGM) has embraced this challenge head-on, instituting a yearslong collaboration with academics from leading business schools to explore how using data and analytics can improve visitors’ experiences.

title: Big Tech accused of stonewalling European social media researchers
summary: Researchers say TikTok, X, and Meta aren't providing data they're legally required to.
full_text:
In the final weeks before Romania’s presidential vote in November 2024, TikTok accounts that had previously spent years posting about manicures or fashion suddenly started promoting a little-known politician named Calin Georgescu.
His posts, espousing hard-line views on immigration and anti-Semitic tropes, were viewed 120 million times before the vote. Georgescu, who had previously been polling in the single digits, stunned observers by winning the election’s first round with 23 percent of the vote.
In the Netherlands, Adriana Iamnitchi was watching closely. As chair of computational social sciences at Maastricht University, she leads the research into disinformation campaigns. She wanted to know how pro-Georgescu content was being monetized on TikTok through hidden influencer marketing and livestreamed political content.
On October 28, 2025, a month before Georgescu won the first round, she and her team applied for access to TikTok’s Application Programming Interface (API) under the EU’s recent Digital Services Act (DSA).
Their request was denied. TikTok said they had failed to prove they were established researchers or to explain their commercial interests or to meet security requirements, Iamnitchi wrote in a blog post.
But two months later, TikTok flagged 116k accounts as potentially compromised before taking action against more than 27,000 fake accounts in a coordinated network run by a third-party “fake engagement vendor” that was promoting Georgescu and his party, the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR). TikTok said it did not know who operated the network or where it originated.
The first round of voting was annulled and in the runoff in May 2025, independent candidate and former Bucharest mayor Nicușor Dan beat AUR’s George Simion, who took over the party after Georgescu was barred from running again. Georgescu said on his YouTube channel that annulling the 2024 results was “practically a formalized coup d’état” by Romania’s Constitutional Court.
Declassified Romanian intelligence showed he “benefited” from massive exposure and preferential treatment by TikTok and that Russia had allegedly coordinated the online campaign to elect Georgescu.

title: India Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan Resigns After CJP, Student Protests
長生駭客 Bryan Johnson 宣稱已經「複製自己」，培養移植用的器官
summary:
7 月 22 日，48 歲的抗老駭客 Bryan Johnson 在 X 上寫下「我剛剛複製了我自己⋯以新生兒 […]

〈長生駭客 Bryan Johnson 宣稱已經「複製自己」，培養移植用的器官〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
7 月 22 日，48 歲的抗老駭客 Bryan Johnson 在 X 上寫下「我剛剛複製了我自己⋯以新生兒的形式」，並說「baby-bryan」目前住在培養皿裡，未來要拿來養器官移植。貼文瘋傳、罵聲四起之後，科學界指出一件更關鍵的事：他描述的是誘導性多能幹細胞（iPSC）技術，這套方法不需要卵子、不會產生胚胎，因此培養皿裡沒有任何新生兒。
（前情提要：Midjourney 推全身超音波掃描器稱媲美 MRI，但放射科專家轟：極度誇大、毫無依據）
（背景補充：生殖醫學重大突破！Conception 成功將「血液」轉化為早期人類卵子，打造 3D 迷你卵巢）
重點摘要
- Bryan Johnson 於 7 月 22 日發文宣稱「複製自己為新生兒」，距他公布罹患自體免疫胃炎僅 21 天
- 他描述的是 iPSC 技術，靠 4 個轉錄因子重程式設計血液細胞，全程不需卵子與胚胎，與桃莉羊的體細胞核轉移完全不同
- Johnson 未公開執行機構、技術資料或第三方驗證，而用 iPSC 養出可移植器官至今仍是再生醫學未解難題
7 月 22 日，一則 X 貼文，開頭只有一句話。
「我剛剛複製了我自己⋯以新生兒的形式。」
I just cloned myself…as a newborn
With this clone, I can:
+ become my own blood boy
+ test therapies on the clone
+ grow organs for transplantation
+ develop new treatments
+ inject young cellsThis baby-bryan lives in a petri dish for now.
This may be scary to some… pic.twitter.com/Ved8ij9Col
— Bryan Johnson (@bryan_johnson) July 21, 2026
發文的是 Bryan Johnson，48 歲，公開表示每年花費約 200 萬美元逆轉生理年齡的矽谷創業家，又被叫做長生駭客。
他接著條列出這個「複製體」的用途：當自己的供血男孩、測試療法、養器官移植、開發新療法、注射年輕細胞。最後一行是，「這個 baby-bryan 目前住在培養皿裡。」
留言區幾個小時內炸開。有人罵他邪惡，有人問這個「孩子」有沒有人權，有人寫下那句被大量轉發的話：想像你出生，只是被當成一個怕死的人的免洗零件。
然後科學界看了那則貼文，指出一件更尷尬的事。
培養皿裡沒有新生兒。連胚胎都沒有。
診斷到複製，中間隔了 21 天
先把時間軸排好。
7 月 1 日，Johnson 公開自己被診斷出自體免疫胃炎，一種免疫系統攻擊胃部泌酸細胞的慢性病，他的說法是「我的胃在吃自己」。這個病無法治癒，會造成鐵與維生素 B12 吸收障礙、貧血並提高胃癌風險，臨床上靠長期補充營養素管理。不可逆，但不是絕症。
7 月 22 日，他宣布自己複製了自己。
中間隔了 21 天。
桃莉羊需要一顆卵子和一隻代理孕母，他兩樣都沒有
真正的複製，技術上叫體細胞核轉移。1996 年在蘇格蘭羅斯林研究所誕生的桃莉羊就是這樣來的。取出一顆卵子，抽掉細胞核，換進一個成體細胞的細胞核，讓它發育成胚胎，再植入代理孕母的子宮。要有卵子，要有胚胎，要有子宮，最後才會有一隻活的羊。
Johnson 描述的是完全不同的東西。
依他本人的說法，那是誘導性多能幹細胞，簡稱 iPSC。做法是抽一管血，把血液細胞放進培養皿，送進四個轉錄因子（Oct4、Sox2、Klf4、cMyc），把這些成熟細胞的分化記憶抹掉，讓它們退回類似胚胎幹細胞的狀態。這套方法由日本科學家山中伸彌在 2006 年建立，2012 年拿下諾貝爾生理醫學獎。
而它得獎的理由，恰好就是它不需要卵子，也不需要胚胎。
所以 Johnson 的培養皿裡是一批被重設過的細胞。沒有胚胎，沒有胎兒，沒有嬰兒，沒有第二個 Bryan Johnson。他列的清單裡，短期內真有實驗室基礎的是「在細胞上測試療法」，因為用 iPSC 做疾病模型與藥物篩選早就是常規操作。至於養出結構完整、可移植的實體器官，那是再生醫學公認最難的一關，連時間表都給不出來。
讓這件事完全合法的，正好是讓這句話不成立的
美國沒有一條聯邦刑法直接把複製人入罪，真正卡住它的是三層：FDA 主張生殖性複製歸自己管轄，並公開表示基於安全疑慮不會核准；聯邦經費禁止投入；另有 9 個州立法禁止，多數禁的是「把複製胚胎植入子宮」這個動作。
Johnson 一步都沒有踩到那條線。
因為 iPSC 從頭到尾不產生胚胎，沒有任何東西可以被植入。他能安全地說出「我複製了自己」，正是因為他做的事情不是複製。
對照組就在七年前。2018 年，賀建奎用 CRISPR 編輯人類胚胎，讓一對雙胞胎女嬰出生，他跨過的正是「細胞」與「人」之間那條線。2019 年 12 月，深圳南山區法院以非法行醫罪判他 3 年有期徒刑，併科罰金 300 萬人民幣。
一個真的越了線，換來 3 年。另一個沒有越線，換來一則瘋傳貼文。
他上一次要年輕血液，物件是 17 歲的兒子
「當我自己的供血男孩」這句話不是隨口說的。
2023 年，Johnson 做過一次三代血漿交換，把當時 17 歲的兒子 Talmage 的血漿輸進自己體內，再把自己的血漿輸給 70 歲的父親。結果也是他自己公布的，檢查一輪生物標記後沒有偵測到任何好處，他停掉這項做法，改做全血漿置換。
這次的差別是，他把年輕細胞的來源從家人換成了培養皿。
而外界能拿到的資訊，就只有那則貼文。他沒有公開執行機構的名稱，沒有發布技術資料，沒有第三方驗證，也沒有同儕審查紀錄。整件事的證據強度，等同於一位當事人在社群平台上的自述。
Theranos 被拆穿的關鍵也不是技術做不到，而是它從不讓外人檢驗自己宣稱做到的事。
Johnson 的病是真的，焦慮大概也是真的。iPSC 也確實扎實、拿過諾貝爾獎、總有一天可能長出可移植組織。
只是那一天還沒到，而培養皿裡的那批細胞，離「新生兒」三個字還隔著整個人類胚胎學。
他沒有複製出一個人。
他複製出來的，是流量。
常見問題
Bryan Johnson 真的複製了一個人嗎？
沒有。他描述的是誘導性多能幹細胞（iPSC）技術，把血液細胞重程式設計回類胚胎幹細胞狀態。這個過程不需要卵子、不產生胚胎，也不會發育成個體。培養皿裡是一批細胞，不是新生兒。
iPSC 現在可以拿來養移植器官嗎？
還不行。iPSC 已能培養出神經、心肌、視網膜等細胞與類器官，用於疾病模型與藥物篩選；但要養出結構完整、可供移植的實體器官，仍是再生醫學最大的未解難題，短期內無法臨床應用。

title: 韓國爭議》7月起圖片上傳先過AI比對，網友轟「網路戒嚴」，官方喊冤不是事前審查
summary:
韓國 7 月 1 日起把《電信事業法》違法拍攝物流通防制的技術性、管理性措施，從影片一路擴大到圖片，約 80 […]

〈韓國爭議》7月起圖片上傳先過AI比對，網友轟「網路戒嚴」，官方喊冤不是事前審查〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
韓國 7 月 1 日起把《電信事業法》違法拍攝物流通防制的技術性、管理性措施，從影片一路擴大到圖片，約 80 家義務業者只要使用者上傳圖片，就得先跟政府認定的資料庫自動比對。導火線是遊戲社群 Ruliweb 管理員 4 月 30 日的一則公告，爭議一路燒到「檢閱國家」的批評，官方則回應這不是事前審查。
（前情提要：全球青少年「社群禁令」浪潮加速，臺灣會跟上嗎？）
（背景補充：歐盟 8 月開鍘：AI 沒「自報身分」最高罰 3% 全球營收，臺灣也在範圍內）
重點摘要
- 7 月 1 日起韓國約 80 家平台上傳圖片須先比對違法拍攝物資料庫，門檻為前年營收 10 億韓元或日均使用者 10 萬人
- 政府給 6 個月宣導期到 12 月 31 日，期間不做行政處分
- Google、Meta、X 都在義務名單內，2025 年 2 月最重的 1,500 萬韓元罰款由 X 收下
韓國 7 月 1 日起把違法拍攝物的過濾範圍從影片擴大到圖片。依《電信事業法》第 22 條之 5，前一年營收 10 億韓元以上、或日均使用者 10 萬人以上的業者，使用者每上傳一張圖片都要先跟政府的數位性犯罪資料庫自動比對，確認不是已認定的違法拍攝物才放行。
韓國廣播媒體通訊委員會（방송미디어통신위원회，前身為放送通訊委員會）點名的義務業者約 80 家，Google、Meta、X、Naver、Kakao 都在名單上，DCInside、Ruliweb 這類大型社群也一起被納入。
引爆討論的不是政府公告，是一則社群公告。遊戲社群 Ruliweb（루리웹）管理員 4 月 30 日發文說明這件事，直言違法拍攝物幾乎不會出現在這類站臺，卻要為此扛下過度負擔。文章擴散後，韓國輿論開始用「檢閱國家」形容整套制度。
政府講了六年的技術義務，最後被一個遊戲論壇的公告推上檯面，這本身就說明制度溝通出過問題。
官方堅持這不是事前審查
主管機關的辯護很直接。官方說法是，圖片比對識別技術「不是直接閱覽內容、也不是事前審查的方式」，只是阻擋已被認定為違法拍攝物的內容再度流通，比對物件限縮在廣播媒體通訊審議委員會審議確定的圖片與影片。
技術上這叫「圖片 DNA」，白話講就是系統不存原圖，只抽出特徵值存庫，再拿新圖去對。裁切、旋轉、翻轉、模糊、變色、加字這些規避手法都要認得出來。政府訂的門檻是偵測率 95% 以上、正常圖片誤擋防止率 95% 以上。
官方也強調這不是新義務。2020 年修法時法條寫的就是「違法拍攝物等」，本來就不分影片圖片，只是技術一直做不到，直到 2025 年 12 月國家層級的開發完成才排進時程。
業者反彈
業者的反彈集中在成本，社群一則貼文動輒夾帶幾十張圖，圖片流量遠高於影片，等於要額外增設高效能 GPU 伺服器，而這筆錢由業者自己吸收，上傳延遲與服務品質下降是連帶結果。
誤判是另一個痛點，已有人擔心同人繪圖或修圖照片被誤攔。反過來看，資料庫裡還沒有的新違法拍攝物，這套機制原本就攔不到，這也是「做給人看」批評的來源。
政府給了 6 個月宣導期，7 月 1 日到 12 月 31 日之間不做行政處分。先上路、罰則往後推半年，這是韓國近年推平台義務的固定節奏。
境外業者到底管不管得到
網路上流傳最廣的說法是這條規定只管韓國國內，境外業者不適用。這點跟事實有落差。
《電信事業法》第 22 條之 5 不分業者國籍，看的是服務規模，韓國國內使用者超過 10 萬人的海外伺服器業者一樣是規管物件。執法紀錄也有，2025 年 2 月 28 日主管機關對 7 家違反義務的業者開罰，最重的 1,500 萬韓元落在海外業者 X 身上，另有 10 多家海外業者收到糾正命令。
真正的破口在別的地方，Telegram 沒被納入，官方理由不是「海外企業」，而是私人對話服務，KakaoTalk 一對一聊天同樣不在範圍。當年 N 號房事件的主要流通管道正是私人對話空間，這才是實效性爭論的核心。
另外一件事，5 月 1 日起大量境外成人網站對韓國連線回傳 HTTP 451 錯誤頁，據韓媒報導這是 Cloudflare 依韓國政府要求做的限制。政府擋內容的手從追個別網站移到跟基礎設施業者合作，這比法條擴大適用更難繞過。
爭議之所以炸開，是因為三件事擠在同一個月。7 月 7 日俗稱假訊息根除法的修正版《資訊通訊網法》上路，日均使用者 100 萬人以上的平台要公布半年度透明度報告，訂閱數 10 萬以上且靠張貼獲利的人故意散布假訊息最高賠損害額 5 倍，重複流通可罰 10 億韓元。7 月 21 日修正版《AI 基本法》再上路，深偽內容要加人眼可辨識標示。
國民力量黨把 7 月 7 日那部法叫「線上封口法」，共同民主黨反駁這是擋惡意假訊息的防禦牆，主管機關強調罰則落在張貼者、不是平台。韓國網友的憤怒可能才開始。
常見問題
韓國 7 月起的圖片過濾規定是什麼？
2026 年 7 月 1 日起，約 80 家韓國義務業者在使用者上傳圖片時要自動比對政府違法拍攝物資料庫，確認不是已登入的違法內容才放行。宣導期到 12 月 31 日，期間不做行政處分。
這項規定對 Google、Meta 等境外平台也適用嗎？
適用。《電信事業法》不分業者國籍，只看服務規模，Google、Meta、X 都在約 80 家義務名單內。2025 年 2 月韓國對 7 家違反義務的業者開罰，其中最重的 1,500 萬韓元罰款由海外業者 X 收下。

title: Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape fires
summary: Families visiting France from the UK and elsewhere have told the BBC how their holidays have become evacuation missions.
full_text:
Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape
- Published
Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.
Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.
Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.
Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.
Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.
Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.
The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".
"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."
Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".
His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11, is still coming to terms with having seen the flames.
"Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."
He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August.
"It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."
Family fled in 15 minutes
David Morton had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun.
But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning.
"Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," he said.
"We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."
He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."
The family has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.
'City is evacuated but I'm still here'
Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.
Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."
She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.
"When I woke up in the morning we were almost alone in the city because the city has been evacuated and I'm still here," she said.
"The main roads are closed because they're on fire - the police advised me on Friday at 07:30 to stay in my home, to not leave my home under any circumstance; there was ash falling from the sky like snow."
Some British families told the BBC they had moved 100 miles away to other parts of France to continue their holidays.
Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born.
"You wouldn't believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 22:00," he said.
Before heading to the Dordogne the family spent a night with hundreds of other evacuees in a gymnasium.
He said he feels lucky to be looked after and safe, but is thinking about holidaying "closer to home" next year.
And BBC South's Joanna Kent, who was on holiday in the Cap Ferret peninsula earlier this week, recalled seeing her campsite deserted after two van loads of police told tourists they had 30 minutes to get out.
While the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.
Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries.
"I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans.
"But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."
In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.
But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.
Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.
