title: Warner Bros. lawsuit accuses Amazon of illegally poaching executives
summary: The lawsuit will likely renew debates about whether term employment agreements are enforceable under California. law
full_text:
Warner Bros. Discovery filed a lawsuit this week accusing Amazon of interference with contractual relations, breach of contract, and unfair competition.
As reported by Deadline, the lawsuit alleges Amazon has been “hurriedly seeking to pirate away a number of contracted employees,” including Pia Barlow, an HBO Max marketing executive who recently joined Amazon MGM Studios. Warner Bros. (whose pending acquisition by Paramount has been paused for at least a few months) said Barlow’s employment contract was “not set to expire until October 31, 2027.”
“In blatant disregard of established California law, Amazon has gone rogue by attempting to induce Plaintiffs’ employees with term employment agreements to breach those agreements with impunity, backed up with the ready assurance that Amazon will defend and indemnify them should they be held to account for their blatantly unlawful acts,” Warner Bros. said.
The company also accused Amazon of seeking to “tortiously induce another WBD employee to breach their term employment agreement, which was not set to expire until December 2027,” although that executive (believed to be HBO programming executive Francesca Orsi) ultimately stayed at Warner Bros.
Deadline noted that this lawsuit is likely to renew debates about whether term employment agreements are actually enforceable under California law.
Amazon MGM Studios declined to comment.

title: The hacker who humiliated spyware makers and was never caught
summary: An awe-inspiring hacktivist who hacked two controversial government spyware makers may be the most prolific hacker to have never gotten caught. What do we know about Phineas Fisher?
full_text:
Over the last few decades, several mysterious hackers have captured the public’s imagination, but none quite like Phineas Fisher. A decade after their most famous hack, Phineas remains, by most accounts, the most prolific and public hacker never to have been caught.
As part of our series on the biggest cybersecurity mysteries of all time, we’re delving into the enigma of Phineas, the hacktivist who hacked controversial spyware makers FinFisher and Hacking Team. The latter, an Italian startup, was among the first to turn government spyware into a viable global business, paving the way for spyware makers such as the Israeli NSO Group. Phineas’ hack against Hacking Team eventually led to the startup’s demise years later.
Apart from Anonymous, an amorphous amalgam of hacktivists with a mixed track record of mostly stunt hacks designed to gather publicity rather than have real impact, Phineas is perhaps the most well-known hacktivist in history. Their story is made of impressive hacks and endless unanswered questions.
Who is Phineas Fisher?
Variously called an anarchist, a cybercriminal, a hacktivist, and a vigilante, the hacker has said they “use a lot of different names” for different hacking escapades.
The hacks we know about were big enough to turn Phineas into a legend among hackers. “I would like to meet Phineas Fisher so that I could buy them a seven-course, three-Michelin-star dinner somewhere and listen to them explain how they turned Hacking Team inside out like a gym sock,” a well-known security researcher once wrote on Twitter. There’s even a song about them.
Phineas first emerged in August 2014, when they announced they had hacked Gamma Group, the makers of the FinFisher spyware — which is where the nickname comes from. They publicized the hack via a Twitter account cheekily called @GammaGroupPR, leaking stolen data including mobile spyware, product manuals, and a price list. The damage was limited, and FinFisher carried on. Phineas published a post-mortem that doubled as a leftist manifesto, then vanished.
A year later, they came back with a bang, hacking Hacking Team, another spyware maker. They took practically everything: more than 400 gigabytes including source code, tens of thousands of internal emails, confidential contracts, and customer lists. The leak allowed journalists to reveal scandals in Ecuador, Mexico, and Panama. Years later, Hacking Team’s CEO David Vincenzetti was forced to sell his company for one euro. For some former employees, Phineas’ hack was the beginning of the end.
Phineas went on to hack the union of the Mossos d’Esquadra, which is the police force of Catalonia, publishing a post-mortem and a 39-minute tutorial video — consistent with their stated anti-police ideals. Their next victim was the ruling party of Turkey’s authoritarian president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a hack motivated by solidarity with Rojava, a leftist autonomous region in northern and eastern Syria that Turkey was fighting against.
Phineas’ last known victim was Cayman National Bank’s branch in the Isle of Man, a self-governing island between England and Ireland. The hack hinted at a different side of Phineas. “I look for illegal ways to make money in order to free my time so I can do something useful with it. Once I had that figured out, I started scaling it up and making more money than I need and giving the extra away,” Phineas said in an interview with activist Freddy Martinez. (Phineas donated at least $10,000 in Bitcoin to Rojava.)
Phineas kept the hack — which happened in 2016 — quiet for three years later before announcing the “Hacktivist Bug Bounty Program,” an initiative to reward hacktivists who expose companies’ illegal and unethical activities. When Cayman National Bank confirmed the hack, it claimed it “was amongst a number of banks targeted.” Phineas confirmed they had been hacking several banks for years.
That was their last public appearance. Their Twitter and Reddit accounts have long since been deleted, leaving no online trail. FinFisher never contacted law enforcement, according to a former company employee. The Italian authorities’ investigation into the Hacking Team hack ended without finding any evidence pointing to Phineas’ real identity. What I can say, from my own reporting, is that Phineas is alive and well — they have been in contact with me within the last couple of years.
So who is Phineas Fisher? Taking their claims at face value, they’re a hacktivist with anarchist ideals, but also a cybercriminal. Could they instead be a fabricated persona controlled by a spy agency — Russia, say, which has a history of inventing hacktivists to muddy the waters after its own hacks? Phineas has denied being a Russian spy, and it’s unclear why Moscow would go after all of Phineas’ chosen targets.
Their origins are equally murky. Phineas has name-dropped Spanish-speaking anarchists, wrote the Hacking Team post-mortem in Spanish, and followed numerous Latin American leftist accounts on Twitter. They told me their first language is neither English nor Spanish, though they have acknowledged living in a Spanish-speaking country. It’s all worth taking with a grain of salt. “Everything I say that contains clues about my identity is half trolling,” Phineas once told me. “I’m in the habit of saying misinformation.”
It’s also possible that the Phineas persona was passed around between 2014 and 2019 and used by different individuals. But there is no evidence of that, and after 10 years of conversations, my gut says Phineas truly is the hacktivist they claim to be.

title: Elon Musk’s Boring Company reportedly raising funding at a $20 billion valuation
summary: Elon Musk's tunneling startup is reportedly in talks for a major new funding round.
full_text:
Elon Musk’s tunneling startup The Boring Company is in talks to raise a $4 billion funding round at a valuation of $20 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.
The deal hasn’t closed and the terms could change, the WSJ says. At $20 billion, the valuation would be a significant increase from The Boring Company’s $5.7 billion valuation in 2022.
The startup has already built a network of tunnels under Las Vegas, through which Teslas shuttle customers to different stations. But tunnel workers have suffered serious injuries, and Nevada regulators said last year that The Boring Company violated environmental regulations nearly 800 times.
The Boring Company has announced plans to build tunnel networks under Nashville and Dubai. The WSJ says the startup has also pitched projects in Baltimore, Chicago, and Los Angeles.
The startup spun out of SpaceX in 2018. SpaceX recently had the largest IPO ever, but its stock price has taken a significant dip since then.

title: Burnham to address social care, youth unemployment and devolution
summary: A No 10 source says it is an attempt by the prime minister to show he is "hitting the ground running".
full_text:
Burnham to address social care, youth unemployment and devolution
- Published
Andy Burnham will make a speech on social care next week as part of what No 10 says is an attempt to show he is "hitting the ground running" as prime minister.
He will also separately address youth unemployment and devolution in the coming week.
Downing Street described the three areas as "some of the most difficult issues facing the country that have been ignored for too long".
Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown. He has vowed to spend political capital on the issue as prime minister.
A No 10 source said: "Andy is going to run towards problems that have been neglected, giving people hope again."
- Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to? - Published1 day ago
 
- Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM - Published4 days ago
 
The source said: "He has the courage to fix the most difficult issues that have been ignored for years and seen as impossible to resolve. He doesn't accept that they are. They can't be ignored any longer.
"The prime minister is determined to show that governments can make people's lives better if they choose to. He wants to get Britain believing again."
Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use, and people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with the cost of care from their local council.
Burnham would not be the first leader in recent years to pledge to address the issue of adult social care.
In 2019, in his first speech as prime minister, Boris Johnson said the Conservative Party would "fix the crisis in social care once and for all".
Five years later in July 2024, Keir Starmer faced criticism when Labour scrapped plans for an £86,000 cap on the amount anyone in England would need to spend on their personal care over their lifetime.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, who has pushed for social care reform, said on Saturday: "This has to be the start of a real effort to end the social care catastrophe."
He added: "I'll fight to ensure family carers aren't forgotten. We need cross-party consensus, and I hope the PM's door is open."
Burnham responded to Sir Ed on X, writing: "It most certainly is, Ed. Let's work together to find some common ground."
Kevin Hollinrake, chairman of the Conservative Party, said: "Where's the money coming from, Andy? We're all dying to know.
"It is all well and good for the prime minister to promise to fix the issues facing our country, but how is he going to pay for them?"
In the first week of his premiership, Burnham has pledged to end rough sleeping in England, cut VAT from domestic electricity bills in the current financial year, and reduce the cap on bus fares outside of London from £3 to £2 from January.
His government also announced it would cut business rates for pubs, clubs, and live music venues in England by 20% from April.

title: Norris cautious despite pole as it 'falls apart' for Hamilton
summary: Lando Norris has an opportunity to win his first grand prix of the year in Hungary, but Lewis Hamilton says his positivity is being tested after another penalty.
full_text:
Norris cautious despite pole as it 'falls apart' for Hamilton
- Published
Lando Norris took his first pole position of the year in Hungary but is cautious about whether he can follow it up with his first victory as world champion.
Perhaps the McLaren driver was casting his mind back to Miami in early May, when he was leading towards the end of the first stint of the race, only for his team to make a strategic misstep and allow Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli to sneak in for a win.
"You can't just rely on one good qualifying, so I need a good race tomorrow," Norris said.
"Then we obviously have a nice summer break, but after that we need to try and repeat it several more times.
"We've been working hard. We know we've been on the back foot, but we're making progress and today certainly shows that."
Much of the attention at the Hungarian Grand Prix has been on the massive upgrade made by Aston Martin on their recalcitrant car, which has provided the troubled team with a major step forward and allowed Fernando Alonso to escape the first qualifying session for the first time all season.
That meant McLaren's own upgrade went under the radar somewhat, but it has been effective.
Still, team principal Andrea Stella, while expressing his satisfaction that the upgrades had enabled them to engage in a fight for pole they did not expect, said Norris' pole was an "overachievement".
McLaren's own good execution of qualifying was one factor, he said, in addition to an under-performance from Ferrari, and perhaps even Antonelli and Mercedes.
Ferrari came into Hungary as most people's favourite, including McLaren's, on the basis that their car is the fastest in the corners, but it lacks engine performance, and this is one of the least power-sensitive tracks on the calendar.
Lewis Hamilton was fastest after the first runs in the final part of qualifying but did not improve on his final lap. Shortly after completing it, he blocked Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri and the stewards imposed a three-place grid penalty.
Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur said the team took responsibility for that because they did not warn Hamilton in time.
The seven-time world champion later posted on Instagram:, external "Sometimes you just can't catch a break. Another weekend when I've been feeling great throughout all the sessions, but then it just falls apart."
Referencing penalties he had been given in the previous two races in Britain and Belgium, Hamilton added: "I always do my best to keep positive - sport is always about the highs and lows, but it's also in the margins.
"Every point counts and you have to seize every opportunity. After three penalties in three weekends, it's becoming difficult to hang on to that positivity.
"Still, I won't let the setbacks take away from the progress we've been making as a team. With the pace we have, I'm hopeful we can get something out of the race tomorrow."
Hungarian Grand Prix
26 July at 14:00 BST
Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app
For all that Ferrari have been quick, Norris and McLaren have also looked in good shape all weekend. And, at least on this circuit, they have vaulted right to the front, into a position that had been familiar for the past two seasons but not so in 2026.
While sat with Ferrari's Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, Norris said: "I knew the pace was certainly there. It has been all weekend. Even though these guys have been insanely fast, I knew I'd been driving very well, I'd been consistent, and I knew the car had potential.
"We also had the upgrades this weekend, and it doesn't feel that different, but it certainly seems to be going a little bit quicker, and that's always a good thing."
Overtaking is expected to be especially difficult around the Hungaroring this year.
In Miami an excess of caution on McLaren's part about the potential of rain allowed Mercedes to pit Antonelli before Norris and leap into the lead.
Norris' pole provides an opportunity to make amends for that - if he can keep Leclerc behind on the run to the first corner.
After winning two consecutive constructors' titles in 2024 and 2025, as well as Norris' drivers' championship last year, McLaren have not had a great season at the start of this new regulation cycle.
Securing the title against a late-season onslaught from Max Verstappen and Red Bull put them behind on designing this year's car, and they took some missteps on aerodynamic philosophy that only became fully understood after the first handful of races.
An upgrade package introduced by McLaren this weekend, their first since Miami, is the fruit of work aimed at correcting course, and the first signs are positive.
They have also struggled to get on top of the operation of the new Mercedes engine, feeling for the first time that they were suffering for not being a works partner of a manufacturer.
"It's just nice to be on pole," said Norris, who had also shown competitive pace in Belgium last weekend but was denied a good result by a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts, and then by bad luck with the timing of a safety car.
"I have felt good all weekend. The last few weekends, honestly, I felt pretty good and it's been nice I continued my good feelings in the car.
"I had my money on Ferrari before the weekend and they have been insanely quick, but, come qualifying, we just seemed to take more of a step forward. I knew it was possible and that has been a good feeling - and one that I have missed for quite a while."
As for his prospects in the race, Norris alluded to strong performances from the Mercedes and Ferrari drivers on the race-simulation runs in Friday practice when he said: "The race pace on others looked very strong. It is always a bit tricky to know how things will go with a new car and new bits."
Leclerc, though, felt Norris would certainly be in the fight, and both have some protection from Hamilton and Antonelli, both demoted by three-place penalties to fifth and seventh respectively.
"Lando seems to be very, very strong, so I'll say Lando [is favourite]," Leclerc said. "But if you look over the course of the season, Mercedes has always been up there, so I do not doubt that they'll all be in the fight as well."

Aston Martin and Alonso take major step
At Aston Martin there was at last some reason to feel positive after a dark time this season.
So much had been expected of the team when design legend Adrian Newey joined in March last year, but a late start to their design process, combined with engine partner Honda falling well short of performance and - like McLaren - some errors in philosophy, have left them cemented at the back all year.
In absolute terms, progressing beyond the first session for the first time all season, and lining up 16th, is nothing special. But to be able to compete with other teams, for pretty much the first time all year, was a major step.
In percentage terms, this was not quite Aston Martin's best performance of the season - they were 0.012% closer to pole in Japan. But it is huge compared with where they have fallen since as others have developed their cars.
There is a Honda engine upgrade to come for the next race after the summer break - of undefined size. More importantly, this has revitalised faith in Aston Martin's development capabilities after three years of upgrades that failed to deliver what the team expected.

title: Gymnast Langton cleared of serious injury after shocking fall
summary: English gymnast Gabriel Langton is cleared of serious injury after a sickening fall at the Commonwealth Games on Friday.
full_text:
Gymnast Langton cleared of serious injury after fall
- Published
English gymnast Gabriel Langton has been cleared of serious injury after a sickening fall at the Commonwealth Games on Friday.
Langton fell head first from three metres to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar during the opening day of competition and was taken to hospital.
Team England said Langton underwent "multiple scans" on Saturday with "very positive results".
The 19-year-old, who has not qualified for any remaining events at the Games, will be discharged from hospital on Saturday evening.
"He is in good spirits and hugely grateful for the many messages of support and the excellent care provided by the medical teams," a statement said.
"He is looking forward to being reunited with the team to celebrate his silver medal."
There was a lengthy halt to proceedings after Langton's fall before he was taken away on a stretcher.
When the competition resumed, his team-mates secured a silver medal behind Canada, though Langton is yet to receive his.
After the incident, team-mate Luke Whitehouse said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."
Canada's Felix Dolci said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.
"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team."
Langton was a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock.

title: Head of Hamas-led police in northern Gaza killed by Israeli strike
summary: Four other Palestinians were also killed by Israeli air strikes, and a policeman died from wounds sustained last week.
full_text:
Head of Hamas-led police in northern Gaza killed by Israeli strike
Four other Palestinians were also killed by Israeli air strikes, and a policeman died from wounds sustained last week.
The head of the Hamas-led police force in northern Gaza has been killed by an Israeli air strike, while other attacks have claimed the lives of five more Palestinians, the Hamas-run interior ministry and medics said.
Brigadier-General Abdel-Nasser Al-Maqadma, who also served as governor of northern Gaza, was targeted in the Sheikh Radwan area north of Gaza City on Saturday. The Israeli military said he had also been a member of the military wing of Hamas.

Israeli strikes also killed a Palestinian medic in the Nuseirat refugee camp, and two people in a house in Khan Younis. Israel’s military said the house was attacked to target a member of the Islamic Jihad group
Later on Saturday, another air strike on Khan Younis killed high school student Khaled Al-Breim. Relatives said he was killed as he sought to bring sweets to distribute to relatives and friends who had flocked into his family home to offer their congratulations as he had just concluded high school and was preparing for university.
A sixth death was a policeman who was wounded by an Israeli strike last week and died from his injuries on Saturday.
In recent months, Israel has killed dozens of members of the Hamas-led police force, alleging that many were tied to Hamas’ armed wing and represented an active threat.
Hamas accuses Israel of deliberately targeting the force to destabilise the enclave, calling it a further breach of the US-brokered ceasefire reached in October.
The ceasefire deal has been mostly ignored by Israel. Since the truce agreement was signed, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,180 Palestinians, mostly civilians, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Over the same period, four Israeli soldiers have been killed in attacks in Gaza.

title: Biden ghostwriter tapes to be released
summary: Former President Joe Biden is declining to appeal a court ruling that allows the Justice Department to publicize recordings of conversations between him and a writer collaborating on his memoir.
full_text:
Biden ghostwriter tapes to be released
Former President Joe Biden will not appeal a court ruling allowing the Trump Justice Department to release transcripts and tape recordings of the Biden's conversations with his ghostwriter.
Biden's lawyers filed a notice of voluntary dismissal Friday in a related case that has the effect of ending the legal battle.
 
The result is a win for the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank that sued in order to publicize the records.
 
The tapes date back to 2017, after Biden left office as vice president and sat for several hours of interviews with the writer collaborating on his memoir, Promise Me, Dad. In 2022, when Biden was president, he informed the Justice Department that he had discovered classified documents at his Wilmington, Del., home. The Department then began an investigation into his handling of classified document; it collected the tapes as a part of that investigation.  
In 2024, Robert Hur, a special prosecutor appointed by the Justice Department concluded that although Biden brought some classified documents to his home, that criminal charges were not warranted. As the special prosecutor's report put it, after reviewing classified documents every day for eight years as Vice President, Biden finding documents at his home "could have been an unremarkable and forgettable event."
The report, however, sparked controversy because it described Biden as "a sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory." And according to the 2024 report, the tapes of Biden's conversations with his ghostwriter were "painfully slow, with Mr. Biden struggling to remember events and straining at times to read and relay his own notebook entries."
Conservative activists seeking the tapes hope that the records will validate concerns about Biden's mental acuity before he was elected president. "What you're going to hear on the tapes … is the state of Joe Biden years before he ran for president, when a special prosecutor said he has memory issues," said Jeffrey Clark, a Trump ally and vice president for litigation at the Oversight Project, one of the law firms involved in the effort to access Biden's 2017 tapes.
Clark adds that conservative organizations involved in the lawsuit plan to immediately publicize the entirety of the tapes and transcripts. "We'll put out a link," he told NPR. "It's not more complicated than that."
At the time of the special prosecutor's report, Biden had not yet bowed out of the 2024 election. He bashed it as "not only misleading, but also plain wrong."
A source familiar with the 2017 tapes says they are "painfully boring" in the sense that Biden is going through documents one-by-one, reading them, and then talking about them.
Biden eventually withdrew from the 2024 presidential race after a disastrous debate performance.
Conservative groups filed their lawsuit in April 2024, and the Department of Justice fought against releasing the tapes for nearly two years, including during the first year of the second Trump administration. The Department argued that such a release would be tantamount to releasing "entries in a personal diary." But in May of this year, the Justice Department reversed course, saying it now intends "to disclose the written transcript and audio recordings."
That prompted Biden to intervene in the lawsuit. His lawyers argued that Biden's privacy interests outweigh the public's interest in hearing the tapes and that multiple laws prevent their release. But two lower courts disagreed, including the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, which refused to grant an injunction that would have blocked the release of the tapes while Biden sought an emergency order from the Supreme Court.
What's more, the appellate court's decision was not along liberal/conservative lines. Ruling against Biden were Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan, an Obama appointee, and Gregory Katsas, a Trump appointee, with Judge Florence Pan, a Biden appointee, in dissent.
Faced with the strong likelihood that the tapes would be released, the Biden team decided to fold its tent, and turn over the tapes and papers to the Heritage Foundation. A Biden source not authorized to speak publicly noted that the Trump Justice Department had abandoned the DOJ's traditional opposition to turning over such material. If private conversations about a book can be obtained by DOJ and turned over to a private, said the source, that is a "dangerous" prescription for how the government can wield its power against individuals.
The Justice Department has not responded to a request for comment.
Biden's decision not to pursue his legal fight further is in sharp contrast to President Trump's take-no-prisoners approach to litigation. Indeed, even as Biden was bowing out of the tapes case, Trump was asking the Supreme Court for a second time to hear his challenge to a jury verdict that requires him to pay E. Jean Carroll $5 million for assaulting her in 1996 and for defaming her after she described the attack in her 2019 memoir. It is extremely rare for the Supreme Court to revisit a case that the justices have already declined to hear. Indeed, the last time the court agreed to hear a case it had previously rejected was in 2018, eight years ago. But unlike Biden, in litigation, Trump never seems to leave a stone unturned.

title: ‘Cockroach Movement’ Forces Out India’s Education Minister
summary: Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday in response to rising pressure from student-led protests.
full_text:
Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday amid mounting pressure from the “Cockroach Movement,” which demanded major government reforms—starting with his departure. Student activists accused Pradhan of failing to safeguard a competitive medical school exam, the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), after authorities concluded that its contents had been leaked online.
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) started as a parody account on social media after Indian authorities invalidated the annual medical school entry exam in May. Its name alludes to a comment made by Chief Justice Surya Kant during an unrelated hearing the same month, in which he compared young unemployed people to "cockroaches” and “parasites.”
However, the CJP quickly established itself as a formidable movement as anti-government sentiment erupted in the wake of the NEET scandal. The page gained millions of followers, and its founder began organizing protests in late June.
How a Leaked Exam Sparked a National Movement
Over 2 million prospective students had taken the three-hour exam, according to the BBC. However, an exam coach noticed that a “guess paper”—or practice test—being circulated online seemed to closely match the exam itself, prompting an investigation. Police ultimately concluded that the questions had been leaked. They also discovered that some individuals paid as much as 5,000 rupees (about $52) to access the “guess paper” on WhatsApp, the Indian Express reported.
News that the exam results had been voided distressed many of the test-takers. The medical school system in India offered fewer than 130,000 slots for the undergraduate medical program this year, according to India’s National Medical Commission, making the selection process extremely competitive. The stakes are considerable, especially for those with limited financial resources. After the exam was discredited, at least 20 students died by suicide, according to Agence France-Presse. Protesters blamed the deaths on what they described as systemic failures in India's education system, and directed much of their anger toward Pradhan.
In a statement posted to social media after he stepped down, Pradhan said that the government would be switching to a computer-based testing model in the future to help prevent fraud and confirmed that a replacement exam had been successfully completed in June.
“India’s youth power is the real strength of this nation,” he wrote.
Without accepting fault, he explained that he had agreed to step down in order to prevent “anti-national forces” from exploiting the upheaval.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP, celebrated the resignation with fellow protesters in New Delhi on Saturday.
“It's a victory for the people of India,” Dipke said to the crowd. He later posted an image of India’s Constitution on social media, with the caption: “Thank you.”
How the Protests Forced the Government to the Table
Despite police orders not to march on Parliament, tens of thousands of protesters attempted to do so last week and clashed with local authorities. The following day, they escalated their efforts by attempting to block public transportation, setting up barricades at the entrance of key metro stations and disrupting travel for millions of daily commuters. The police used tear gas and batons to disperse protesters, sparking public outrage.
Activist Sonam Wangchuk was then forcibly taken to hospital after 26 days of a hunger strike meant to bring attention to protesters’ demands. He told local media outlets that he concluded his campaign after receiving assurances that the “issue of accountability” for the failures of the exam would be discussed by Parliament.
Upon hearing the news of the Education Minister’s resignation on Saturday, he told reporters that he welcomed the move.
"This is a victory for democracy that we witnessed today,” he said. “I congratulate and thank our CJP team who first raised this issue, as well as the volunteers who supported them, the students, youth, and elders from across the country who stood up for democracy.”
"I hope we maintain this peace and that no wrongdoing occurs anywhere in the future. We need to work on reforms. A nation isn't built by resignation alone," he added.
On the advice of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Indian President Droupadi Murmu appointed Pralhad Joshi—who already oversees the ministries of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, along with New and Renewable Energy—to oversee the Ministry of Education “in addition to his existing portfolio,” which is a typical arrangement in India following a Cabinet vacancy and does not preclude a later permanent appointment.
Joshi addressed the exam leak in May, saying, “The reforms are needed, we are bringing them, but they cannot be done within a year. By next year, technology-driven examination will be there."
CJP Spokesperson Saurav Das said in an interview with local media ANI following the president’s announcement that the party members will be meeting the new education minister “very soon.”
“Whoever becomes the Education Minister should know that the youth are watching. They will demand accountability,” Das said. “So, when the time comes, work in the interest of the youth. Stop paper leaks.”
What Comes Next for the CJP?
The CJP established its list of demands on May 16. In addition to calling for Pradhan’s resignation, the CJP asked for compensation of 10 million rupees ($104,000) for each student who died by suicide following the leak.
They also sought greater legislative oversight of the educational system, gender equity in government roles, a fully independent media, and certain reforms to the electoral and political system—such as creating a 20-year ban on politicians switching parties before seeking election.
Adding to those mandates, the CJP last week asked that the central government drop any potential charges against protesters, after claiming that several had been “illegally detained” by police.
Following Pradhan’s resignation, representatives from the CJP met with officials from the Indian government to discuss the rest of the party’s demands. In a press conference following the meeting, Das said on Saturday that the negotiations had been successful.
"All our demands have been accepted,” he said, without elaboration. “We request the protesters to withdraw immediately and return home peacefully."
The CJP added during the press conference on Saturday that representatives from the movement would meet with officials again in four weeks to work on broader reforms. Its spokesperson told local media that the fight for a transparent educational system is far from over.
He said that members of the CJP conveyed to officials that if the issues are not addressed, the protesters will reconvene “and demand accountability.”

title: Robinhood in talks with Crypto.com over prediction markets: WSJ
summary: While prediction market companies in the US continue to face legal battles between state and federal authorities, Robinhood is reportedly considering expanding its services.
full_text:
Robinhood in talks with Crypto.com over prediction markets: WSJ
While prediction market companies in the US continue to face legal battles between state and federal authorities, Robinhood is reportedly considering expanding its services.
The company behind the cryptocurrency and stock trading app, Robinhood, is reportedly discussing plans to expand its existing prediction markets offering with crypto exchange Crypto.com.
According to a Friday Wall Street Journal report citing people familiar with the matter, Robinhood was in talks with Crypto.com to place yes-or-no event contracts supplied by the exchange. The trading company launched its prediction markets hub in March 2025, initially facilitated by Kalshi in order to comply with regulatory requirements from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and later using ForecastEx and Rotella.
The reported move came just days after Bernstein analysts raised the firm’s price target on Robinhood (HOOD) stock to $160 from $130 per share, based on the company’s outlook for prediction markets and tokenized equities. They predicted Robinhood’s revenue using prediction markets could reach $1.7 billion by 2028.
While Bernstein said in April that volumes in prediction markets could reach $1 trillion by 2030, many of the platforms face ongoing legal challenges in the United States between state and federal authorities. The CFTC has claimed to have “exclusive jurisdiction” over the companies’ event contracts, while gaming authorities in many states have filed lawsuits attempting to block or restrict their activities.

title: EU adds HTX to Russia sanctions list, barring transactions starting Aug. 23
summary: Other crypto platforms listed alongside HTX include EXMO, Rapira, BitPapa, Aifory Pro, WhiteBird, NoOnecrypto and Exnode.
full_text:
EU adds HTX to Russia sanctions list, barring transactions starting Aug. 23
Quick Take
- The European Union added HTX to a list of third-country financial and crypto service providers accused of helping Russia circumvent sanctions, with a transaction ban set to take effect on Aug. 23.
- The measure does not impose an asset freeze, but generally bars people and companies in the EU from dealing directly or indirectly with the exchange.
- The bloc also created a broader mechanism to prohibit dealings with crypto platforms based in countries that repeatedly fail to prevent Russian sanctions evasion, although no countries have yet been added.
- Other crypto platforms listed alongside HTX include EXMO, Rapira, BitPapa, Aifory Pro, WhiteBird, NoOnecrypto and Exnode, among others.
We'd love your feedback.
The European Union has added crypto exchange HTX to its Russia sanctions regime, prohibiting people and companies in the bloc from transacting with the platform beginning next month.
The EU identified "HTX (HUOBI GLOBAL SA)" among a group of third-country financial institutions and crypto service providers that it said were significantly frustrating restrictions imposed over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, according to a regulation published in the bloc’s Official Journal. The restriction takes effect on Aug. 23.
Under the applicable rules, EU operators will be barred from engaging directly or indirectly in transactions with HTX. The measure stops short of a full designation or asset freeze, Reuters reported. Eligible EU, European Economic Area and Swiss nationals and residents may seek authorization to withdraw funds or close accounts, but must apply within three months of the ban taking effect.
The legal document’s identification of the exchange as "HTX (HUOBI GLOBAL SA)" contrasts with a statement an HTX spokesperson gave The Block after the United Kingdom sanctioned Huobi Global S.A. in May. The spokesperson said at the time that Huobi Global S.A. was distinct from HTX.
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, first announced the sanctions package in June and said it would extend to 20 non-EU entities, including banks, crypto platforms, and oil traders that have been servicing sanctioned Russian entities and individuals, but did not name HTX at the time.
The UK said it had reasonable grounds to suspect that Huobi Global S.A. supported the Russian government by providing financial services or making funds and other resources available to A7 Limited Liability Company, a Russia-linked cross-border payments firm. HTX said following the British action that regulatory compliance remained an "absolute top priority" and that it adhered to the rules in jurisdictions where it operated.
The EU action also comes two days after blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs alleged that HTX had been rotating hot wallets and funding addresses across TRON, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Solana following the UK sanctions. TRM said addresses were rotated and retired within hours, making screening systems built around static sanctions lists less effective.
HTX rejected TRM’s characterization, telling The Block that the wallet movements reflected "routine, security-driven platform operations common across the industry."
The HTX restriction forms part of the EU's 21st sanctions package against Russia, which was adopted on July 23. The package designated 218 individuals and entities, the largest batch of listings in four years, while separately expanding transaction restrictions covering banks, crypto platforms, oil traders and other entities. The Council said it also added four designations tied to the A7 network and extended its transaction ban to 14 crypto-related service platforms.
Other crypto platforms listed alongside HTX include EXMO, Rapira, BitPapa, Aifory Pro, WhiteBird, NoOnecrypto and Exnode. The restrictions against those platforms are also scheduled to take effect on Aug. 23.
The package goes beyond targeting individual exchanges. A new provision allows the EU to prohibit transactions with crypto service providers established in a country that has "systematically and persistently" failed to stop platforms from undermining the bloc’s sanctions. The accompanying annex naming countries subject to that restriction is currently empty, meaning the EU has established the mechanism without yet applying it to an entire jurisdiction.
HTX did not immediately respond to The Block's request for comment on the EU action. The exchange was founded as Huobi in China in 2013 and is closely associated with Tron founder Justin Sun, whom HTX has described as an adviser.

title: SDCC teaser gives us our first good look at Blade Runner 2099
summary: Also: Forging the One Ring in Rings of Power S3 teaser; new Lanterns trailer; Spaceballs: The New One panel.
full_text:
It’s been nearly five years since Ridley Scott first announced his plans for a TV spinoff of his sci-fi masterpiece Blade Runner (1982) and the 2017 sequel Blade Runner 2049. It’s finally here—or almost, anyway. Prime Video debuted the first teaser for the new ten-episode series, Blade Runner 2099, at San Diego Comic-Con on Friday. We also got a teaser for the third season of Prime Video’s Rings of Power and a new trailer for HBO’s Lanterns.
Yeoh and Schafer joined show runner Silka Luisa (Shining Girls) onstage for the big reveal, which also included an exclusive clip shown to the audience. Luisa told Entertainment Weekly that the series stays true to the original’s “noir principles… and there’s a mystery at the heart of the show that looks both forwards and backwards in terms of mythology.” An uprising has occurred and the humans lost, which means they are now the hunted second-class citizens. “The show is really imagining what comes after us, and what does it mean to be human in a world where humanity is no longer relevant,” said Luisa.
Per the official synopsis:
Fifty years after the events of Blade Runner 2049, Los Angeles has been reborn, just not by humanity. Cora, a fugitive in a final bid to stop running, takes on one last identity: a Blade Runner. Forced to partner with Olwen, a Replicant days from dying, she hunts down a runaway hiding a truth that could collapse their fragile city.
The incomparable Michelle Yeoh stars as Olwen, the dying Replicant, along with Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) as Cora. The cast also includes Hugo Hamlet as Buster Friendly, as well as Dmitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Katelyn Rose Downey, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, Amy Lennox, Sheila Atim, Matthew Needham, Tom Burke, and Maurizio Lombardi—all in as-yet-undisclosed roles.
Blade Runner 2099 will premiere on November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.
Rings of Power S3
Prime Video made a major investment in The Rings of Power when it acquired the rights to the source material from the Tolkien estate, even committing to multiple seasons upfront. We’re now coming up on S3 and based on the teaser the streaming platform unveiled at SDCC, we’ll finally get to see Sauron (Charlie Vickers) forging the One Ring.

title: Littler sets up Price final at World Matchplay
summary: Luke Littler is on course to beat Phil Taylor's tournament average record after another impressive victory saw him reach the final.
full_text:
Littler sets up Price final at World Matchplay
- Published
Defending champion Luke Littler strolled into the World Matchplay final with a 17-5 demolition of unseeded Dirk van Duijvenbode in Blackpool.
The world number one raced in an 8-2 advantage and was averaging 117.10 and on course to beat Phil Taylor's tournament match average record of 114.99
Littler admitted afterwards that distracted him and his level did drop slightly as he finished with an average just below 111.
However, that leaves him well placed to beat Taylor's tournament average of 106.31, with Littler's currently at 110.88.
The teenager's victory also means he has now amassed more than £3m in the PDC's order of merit, and is more than £2m clear of world number two Luke Humphries.
Littler will face Wales' Gerwyn Price in Sunday's final after he beat Netherlands' Gian van Veen 17-10.
Sunday's final gets under way at 20:05 BST, with the Women's World Matchplay taking place in the afternoon session from 13:00 – Beau Greaves and defending champion Lisa Ashton the top two seeds.
Price replaces Clayton as Welsh number one
Price broke in the opening leg of the game and charged into a 4-1 lead, before a scrappy run of legs saw both players break throw regularly to leave Price leading 11-9 at the final mini-break.
From there, the seventh seed powered on and stretched away from Van Veen in scoring and finishing to seal a comfortable victory.
Both players missed 23 darts at a double across the match, while Van Veen was broken nine times in 14 legs throwing first on what was a difficult night for the world number three.
The victory sees Price climb to fourth in the order of merit, above Jonny Clayton, and in turn becomes Welsh number one.
Price told Sky Sports he was "happy" to reach the final, but "getting one up" on good friend Clayton was his main focus going into the tie.
Follow live text coverage of the men's World Matchplay on the BBC Sport website and app from 19:30 BST on Sunday.

title: 'He'll go right through this guy' - Joshua v Prenga predictions
summary: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's heavyweight fight between Anthony Joshua and Kristian Prenga.
full_text:
Joshua v Prenga - heavyweight predictions
- Published
Anthony Joshua returns to the ring on Saturday against the relatively unknown Kristian Prenga in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, knowing that victory would set up a long-awaited showdown with Tyson Fury.
Joshua, a two-time world champion and Olympic gold medallist, has won 29 fights - 26 by stoppage - and lost four.
Albanian Prenga enters the fight with an impressive record of his own, having achieved all of his 20 victories with stoppages while suffering only one defeat.
However, the 35-year-old has never faced anyone close to Joshua's level.
After Fury comfortably dispatched Polish veteran Mariusz Wach in Thailand on Friday, can Joshua can come through his own warm-up bout?
This will be Joshua's first fight since he was involved in a car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of two close friends, Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele.
The Fury-Joshua fight has been a decade in the making. Contracts have been signed, with the blockbuster bout expected to take place later this year.
But could Prenga spoil the party and pull off a huge shock to go down in boxing history as the man who got in the way of Joshua-Fury happening?
Radio commentary from Jeddah will begin from about 20:30 BST on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, and the BBC Sport website and app.
Live text commentary will begin at 19:30 on the BBC Sport website and app.
BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for Saturday's fight.
Natasha Jonas - former two-weight world champion
"I think AJ will win by a stoppage late. He has to be careful at the beginning of the fight because a lot of Prenga's stoppages have come in the first couple of rounds - he rarely goes past six rounds, so that's uncharted territory."
Prediction - Joshua
Carl Frampton - former two-weight world champion
"I think AJ will have a look in the first round but it will be over round three or four. I think he'll go right though this guy. I hope he does and we see him and Fury."
Prediction - Joshua
- Ready to 'conquer Earth' - Joshua embraces comeback spotlight - Published2 days ago
 
- Joshua v Prenga - all you need to know - Published4 days ago
 
Josh Kelly - IBF light-middleweight world champion
"Joshua coming back from what he has is a testament to himself. His attitude and mental resilience. I haven't seen much of Prenga, but I've heard he's a tough guy. If the right Anthony Joshua goes out there and performs, he's a hard night for anyone. If he goes out and performs, he can put anyone on their back. He needs to not overthink. Do your job, get in and get out."
Prediction - Joshua
Adam Smith - DAZN commentator
"Obviously it's been an incredibly difficult time for AJ but he seems mentally and physically in a good place, training under Team Usyk.
"I expect him to go out there and emphatically deal with Prenga, who has not fought at anywhere near Joshua's level. So Joshua to win within the first four rounds."
Prediction - Joshua
Adam Booth - trainer
"I think it's a fascinating opponent for AJ to take, because although you may criticise Prenga's style and that it might not look the best, he was a tough unbeaten kickboxer. We saw with Rico Verhoeven against Usyk that these kickboxers can make it tough. I expect AJ to look fresh, establish a quick jab early and have attention to detail.
"He looks very lean, I think he'll be quicker than before and I think he's going to get a clean win. Prenga will try but I think AJ will walk him on to a shot."
Prediction - Joshua
Barry Jones - former super-featherweight world champion
"In recent times, you're never quite sure which version of Joshua would turn up on the night.
"But saying that, any version of Joshua will have too much for Prenga. He's big and powerful, but I think he's out of his depth.
"I think Joshua will be a little bit more confident and forceful against this level of opposition. I think it will be three or four rounds before Joshua gets to him with a stoppage."
Prediction - Joshua
Tony Bellew - former cruiserweight world champion
"You will not see a third round. Joshua will win by a brutal, nasty and vicious knockout."
Prediction - Joshua
Darren Barker - former middleweight world champion
"I predict a brutal Joshua win, early. It won't go past three rounds. Do not blink."
Prediction - Joshua
Dave Coldwell - trainer
"AJ will win whenever he wants - it's a run-out for him. Prenga has a flattering record, but if you look at his style, he's pretty cumbersome. Prenga will walk on to shots but AJ's class, his jab and his power punch will have a massive impact. It depends if Joshua wants a few rounds and to practise what he's been doing with his new team.
"It will last as long as Joshua wants it to - maybe four or five rounds."
Prediction - Joshua
Ade Oladipo - DAZN presenter
"AJ will win by knockout between rounds three and five."
Prediction - Joshua
Anthony Crolla - former lightweight world champion
"Like most, I'll be honest, I've not seen much of Prenga, but what I have seen, it's a gigantic step up.
"The last 12 to 18 months outside the ring and in with the Dubois defeat being a bad one, Joshua can be excused for this type of opponent.
"With AJ and the power he carries, it could be over in a matter of seconds. I expect him to take his time a little bit and for him to knock Prenga out in three rounds."
Prediction - Joshua

title: The West is debating AI’s future with half the world absent
summary:
On July 13, more than 200 leading economists and AI researchers, including 16 Nobel laureates, signed an open letter organised by the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. Its warning was stark: artificial intelligence may drive an economic transformation “larger than the Industrial Revolution” compressed into a fraction of the time, and that we “must act now” to build the institutions to steer it.
We agree with every word. Then we scanned the signatory list. Four in five signatories come from the...
full_text:
On July 13, more than 200 leading economists and AI researchers, including 16 Nobel laureates, signed an open letter organised by the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. Its warning was stark: artificial intelligence may drive an economic transformation “larger than the Industrial Revolution” compressed into a fraction of the time, and that we “must act now” to build the institutions to steer it.
We agree with every word. Then we scanned the signatory list. Four in five signatories come from the United States and Canada, and the rest almost entirely from Europe. Not one name comes from China.
The letter writes about a global economic transformation, but its signatory list suggests half the AI world does not exist. China is home to roughly half of all frontier model development and has arguably the world’s fastest AI adoption. Trying to understand this transformation while excluding China is like studying the Industrial Revolution while ignoring the country with the most factories.
No one intended the omission. It reflects a two-level information gap that runs deeper than most Western observers realise.
The first level is of the AI models themselves. Western businesses are already ahead of Western discourse here. DoorDash, Siemens and Airbnb have adopted Chinese models from DeepSeek, Z.ai (Zhipu AI) and Moonshot AI alongside, and sometimes instead of, their American counterparts.
For cost-conscious companies and governments, the sensible choice is often an open-weight model that runs cheaply on local hardware. Today, that choice is a Chinese model. With the recent release of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, which matches leading US models on many benchmarks, that trend will only accelerate. Investors grasped this immediately: US chip stocks fell on the news.

title: Iran-backed Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia as regional tensions escalate
summary:
Saudi air defences intercept ballistic missiles as Iran reports first night without US strikes in two weeks

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week.

Iran, meanwhile, reported no strikes overnight on Saturday for the first time after two weeks of US attacks. The Iranian health ministry spokesperson, Hossein Kermanpour, said: “Iran had a peaceful night” in a post on X. Tensions, however, remain high.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week.
Iran, meanwhile, reported no strikes overnight on Saturday for the first time after two weeks of US attacks. The Iranian health ministry spokesperson, Hossein Kermanpour, said: “Iran had a peaceful night” in a post on X. Tensions, however, remain high.
A memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran in June seemed to break down two weeks ago, after Iranian attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz prompted US strikes on Iran, which led to Iranian retaliation against US allies in the region. 
 The MoU was meant to reopen the strait after its closure by Iran during the war and pause hostilities for 60 days to give room for negotiations, but active fighting has prevented progress in talks. Much of the current fighting has centred on the strait, a transit point for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas prior to the war.
The US president, Donald Trump, threatened expanded strikes on Iran, meeting top national security advisers on Friday to decide whether the administration should escalate attacks.
He has warned he could widen the scope of targets in Iran to include civilian infrastructure such as Iranian energy plants and bridges, as well as launch a ground operation to seize Kharg Island, one of Iran’s largest oil export terminals.
“There’s a military exit where we just keep going just the way we are, and we can even make it a heavier dose, and it’s knocking out everything they have. Or there’s a smarter strategy that you make a deal,” Trump told reporters on Friday.
Iran issued warnings to citizens of Gulf countries hosting US military sites to stay away from bases to protect themselves from future attacks.
On Saturday night, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that Britain would become a “definite and legitimate target” if it supported the US in any war with Tehran, according to the Iranian state broadcaster, Irib.
The spokesperson said any country, including Britain and Gulf states, that backed the US in a conflict would be considered a legitimate target, adding that US bombers had recently used British airfields.
Trump insisted on Friday that, despite the fighting, negotiations with Iran were going well, calling them “by far the most serious that we’ve seen”.
The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the “American approach” was preventing peace talks from proceeding, while vowing Iran was “neither intimidated by threats nor will we yield to pressure”.
Tensions over the strait continued, with the US firing on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman which it said was violating its blockade of Iranian ports, while the UK maritime agency reported an incident between a tanker and military forces on Friday, without specifying the responsible parties.
Air defence systems in Saudi Arabia intercepted two ballistic missiles from Yemen on Saturday, Reuters reported. The attacks targeted oil refineries in Yanbu on the Red Sea, while the Saudi civil defence also issued warnings for the port city of Jizan, close to the border with Yemen.
A video circulating on social media showed dark clouds rising above a refinery in Jizan belonging to Aramco, the Saudi oil giant. A Yemeni security source told Agence France-Presse a naval base in Hodeida and a military camp on Kamaran island were targeted by Saudi Arabia on Friday. The Houthis said the attacks were a “dangerous escalation”.
The Iran-aligned Houthi movement, which controls northern and western Yemen, declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last week after the kingdom struck the airport in Sana’a. The Houthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea on Thursday, prompting Trump to threaten a “major military punishment” for Tehran and the Houthis.
The naval blockade threatens to further upend global energy markets, as Saudi Arabia has been avoiding the closure of the strait by diverting millions of barrels of oil to the Red Sea. Oil prices pushed past $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May, while the cost of shipping insurance through the southern Red Sea doubled for some companies.
Araghchi said on Saturday that there was no military solution to the Saudi-Houthi conflict and that it was “rooted in old disputes”.
“We believe that there is no military solution to the issue of Yemen, Bab al-Mandab and other regional issues,” Araghchi said in an interview with an Iranian newspaper. He called for further dialogue between the two sides.
Mediators have tried to keep talks alive amid the escalating fighting, Pakistan and Qatar delivering messages between the US and Iran over the last two weeks. The New York Times reported that Iraq had delivered a ceasefire proposal to Tehran, which was promptly rejected – a report disputed by Iraq.
Pakistan has also reportedly been pushing for fresh talks between the two sides after a diplomatic initiative by China explored new dialogue. Iran’s interior minister, Eskandar Momeni, visited Istanbul this week to discuss the topic, reports said.

title: What Love Island tells us about the changing face of dating
summary: From women making the first move to shifting relationship dynamics, Love Island has become a window into Britain's evolving dating culture
full_text:
On the fourth series of Love Island UK in 2018, Megan Barton-Hanson pulled fellow Islander, Wes Nelson, for a chat.
Just moments earlier, she had ended her relationship with Eyal Booker after admitting the pair had little more than physical chemistry. Now, sitting opposite Wes, who had been coupled up with Laura Anderson since the start of the competition, she decided not to wait for him to make the first move.
"I think it's pretty obvious that I do really fancy you," she told him. "And I just felt like, if I didn't say something, I'd regret it massively."
By the end of the episode, viewers had a new nickname for her: "Muggy Megan". Critics accused her of moving too quickly between relationships and breaking "girl code". Others admired her honesty.
At the time, Barton-Hanson argued that she had been treated differently to her male counterparts. "People definitely do give girls a harder time than men… It's sexist."
But eight years later, scenes like Barton-Hanson's no longer feel quite so out of the ordinary. Until this series, the opening coupling had always seen the men choose first. This year, the shows rules were changed, with the women making the first choice.
Alicia Denby, a sociologist at Manchester Metropolitan University, argues the show's tweak is reflective of a broader societal change where "women may now be more likely to approach someone first".
At its peak, around five million people tuned in to Love Island every night. Live audiences are not what they were, but it remains ITV's biggest programme among 16 to 34-year-olds.
For Prof Kitty Nichols, who researches relationships and popular culture at the University of Sheffield, Love Island has become "an important cultural vehicle" allowing us to "reflect on the dating scene and culture at the moment".
Former PE teacher Kai Fagan met his now wife, Sanam Harrinanan, when he won the 2023 series, an experience he says transformed his life.
"My life ever since then has been a fairytale. The whole show is about love. That's the point of it. You're put in a situation to fall in love."
For Fagan, the show delivered exactly what it promised: love. Meanwhile, for thousands watching at home, it has become a window into how modern relationships are formed, tested and understood.
As another series of Love Island approaches its end, what do Love Island's changing dynamics tell us about dating culture beyond the villa? And does women making the first move really represent genuine progress towards equality?
The forever changing rules
For much of the 20th Century, heterosexual dating followed a script that would have felt familiar to the characters in Pride and Prejudice. Men were largely expected to make the first move. They asked women out, paid for dates and, in many cases, took the lead in deciding when the relationship moved forward.
By the 1960s, the women's liberation movement began challenging many of those norms. As Aretha Franklin's Respect became an anthem for a generation demanding greater equality, the widespread availability of contraception changed the ideas about sex. Then with the rise of online dating in the 2000s, millions of people began meeting through websites and, later, dating apps.
But whether these changes have really done anything to shift gender expectations is unclear.
As recently as 2021, sociologist Ellen Lamont reviewed more than 100 studies on heterosexual dating and found traditional dating scripts still remained, with men still expected to make the first move.
For cultural commentator Coco, who goes by her first name and has amassed more than 100,000 followers on TikTok analysing Love Island, this reflects an important distinction.
She argues women aren't replacing men as the pursuers, they simply have greater freedom to act on what they want.
"Women haven't flipped the roles," she says. "Women have just been allowed to exist." She believes women now have "more choice, freedom and opportunity than we've ever had in history".
Love Island's contradiction
But even if women are becoming more comfortable making the first move, Denby argues that this does not mean gendered power relations have disappeared.
She argues that women on Love Island are often praised for their patience and loyalty while male contestants explore connections with other contestants. But she says when women take a more active role in pursuing relationships, they are judged differently.
"It's almost as if women are praised for being submissive in the villa, because when they do take on more of an active or expressive role, they are criticised for it."
On this year's Love Island, in a move that may have reflected the growing trend of women on the show taking the lead, Elicia Bailey took both Aidan Murphy and Finley Maddock to the Hideaway, the villa's private romantic room.

title: Ramsay-Peaty in tears after missing out on gold again
summary: An emotional Adam Ramsay-Peaty questions how his future looks after missing out on gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
full_text:
Ramsay-Peaty in tears after missing out on gold again
- Published
After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.
It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it.
"I work a lot harder than what it says on the scoreboard," the Englishman said after taking 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games, his eyes and cheeks red with emotion.
"It hurts too much. I have got to approach training differently now because it hurts too much."
Ramsay-Peaty has done it all in this sport.
Three Olympic gold medals. Eight world titles. The 14 fastest times in history.
But after taking a break from swimming amid a wave of mental health issues in 2023, he is still searching for that winning feeling again on the big stage.
He was pipped to Olympic gold in Paris two years ago. In Glasgow, despite coming into the final as the fastest qualifier, he had to settle for bronze.
He was beaten by Australia's Sam Williamson but also Jersey's history-maker Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old he has taken under his wing.
Ramsay-Peaty was third at halfway and could not close the gap. His time - 59.65 seconds - was more than four-tenths slower than his semi-final swim and three seconds off his personal best from seven years ago.
"It took a lot of courage to get back into the sport, so we should be happy with everything we get, but then that contradicts the athlete inside me and what I work for," he said.
"I just think I deserve more. I know sport isn't about what you deserve or even what you work for - it's who gets it on the day.
"I just know I'm a better athlete than that. It's very disappointing."
Ramsay-Peaty has spoken about the difficult decisions that come with being an elite athlete. The time away from his son, whom he held in his arms after the Paris silver. The events at home he has to miss.
"They are not even sacrifices; they are choices," he said.
"It's like getting knocked out in the group stages in the World Cup for a very good team. You know you're better and it hurts because you know you have to wait for a very long time for the next championships.
"This is probably - realistically - my last Commonwealth Games and I thought I'd trained for better. I could do better. I've been faster this season. That's where the frustration is."
Ramsay-Peaty has made no secret of the fact he is still competing in the quest for Olympic gold.
He considered retirement again after Paris, but committed to another four years when the 50m race was added to programme for Los Angeles 2028.
This 100m breaststroke is his event - the one in which he went unbeaten in eight years - but there may be a time when he has to let it go.
The 50m race - a dash down one length of the pool - would be less taxing on the body, and Ramsay-Peaty is due back in the pool for that event on Sunday morning.
"Is the 100 even viable any more? I don't know," he said.
"When it hurts like this, the 50 is probably my super strength with my power.
"With the Olympics, that's probably going to be more realistic, but it's too early to tell.
"I just feel like I couldn't have given more this cycle. If I had given less, would it have even equalled more?"
Given the emotion, there are times you wonder how close Ramsay-Peaty is to walking away entirely.
He appeared to walk to the edge but always turned back, insisting the drive for LA remains.
"Of course," he said.
"I know I'm a sprinter. I know I can do very well because I've done it. It doesn't disappear overnight.
"It requires me to look at the formula and see how I can get to that speed again."

title: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questions
summary: The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.
full_text:
I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questions
- Published
I was only a year old when the UK's deadliest terror attack shocked the world.
In December 1988, Pan Am flight 103 exploded over the Scottish town of Lockerbie, killing all 259 people on board as well as 11 on the ground.
I was a teenager by the time Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001 and, when he later died, I thought that was largely the end of the story.
It wasn't.
The case still rumbles on and, later this year, a man suspected of making the bomb which blew up the plane, Abu Agila Masud, goes on trial in Washington DC.
As part of a Radio 4 Intrigue podcast series, I had an opportunity to delve into this complex case with fresh eyes.
The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.
Jim Swire, on the other hand, is sure what he believes - and it is not the official story.
His daughter Flora died in the bombing, but he is convinced that whoever killed her got away with mass murder.
Swire believes Megrahi is innocent, even befriending the convicted bomber up until his death in 2012.
"The burning issue was to get to the truth," he says.
"Always has been, always will be and I will not shut up about what I know to be true."
Swire's doggedness has made him a prominent voice but most of the Lockerbie victims' families don't agree that Megrahi's conviction was a miscarriage of justice - and the bomber’s own appeals against the verdict either failed or were abandoned.
For Swire, the simplest explanation is that Iran was behind the attack - not Libya.
The Lockerbie bombing came five months after 290 people were killed when an Iranian commercial airliner was shot down by a US battleship.
Iran swore revenge and months later Pan Am flight 103 exploded on its way to New York.
And there's more.
Iran - much like they do now - used proxy militant groups to pursue their ends.
Before the Lockerbie bombing, a militant cell based in Frankfurt, part of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine - General Command (PFLP-GC), was foiled by German police.
Police arrested suspects and seized explosive devices, concealed in radio cassette players, that were designed to trigger at altitude.
The bomb that brought down Pan Am 103 was in a radio cassette player hidden inside a samsonite briefcase.
Because of this, Swire believes the device that brought down Pan Am 103 was loaded at Frankfurt, and not Malta as the court had concluded.
And, for Swire, this is only the tip of the iceberg.
He also questions much of the evidence presented at the 2001 trial, discredits witnesses, and is extremely suspicious of the involvement of intelligence agencies - like MI5, MI6 and the CIA - in the aftermath of the bombing.
Combine these suspicions with his all-consuming grief and you can see why Swire is such a force to be reckoned with on his quest for a truth he believes has been denied to him.
"Discovering the truth became my way of handling the consequences of the grief reaction," Swire says.
"And it was very tough for other people to understand that but that's just the way I'm made, I suppose."
Intrigue: Lockerbie
On 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing?
Dick Marquise, who led the FBI's Lockerbie task force, says that in the early days of the case he too believed the PFLP-GC were the "number one suspect", but years of investigation found nothing to prove it.
"There was not one shred of evidence that could be taken to court and get a conviction," he says. "You couldn't do it. There was nothing."
However, there are others, besides Swire, who still question the "official narrative" - including former CIA agent John Holt who also believes Iran was behind the bombing.
Holt worked with Libyan intelligence assets in the 1980s and was the handler of double agent Abdul Majid Giaka, whose information became central to the investigation into the Lockerbie bombing.
Holt now believes Giaka was a "BS artist" who was out for money and was feeding the CIA fake stories to get paid.
"I didn't think much of him at all," he says.
"He gave us some little tidbits about what was going on, but he never knew anything about the Pan Am bombing. And he knew a lot about Megrahi," Holt says.
Holt believes the fact the CIA bankrolled Giaka devalues him as an informant.
"It makes it easier for somebody to say whatever the person who's giving them money wants them to say," Holt says.
I managed to get a hold of the CIA papers - known as cables - from the time, which showed what Giaka had told the Americans.
The cables date back to the months before Lockerbie and include notes of conversations between Giaka and Holt and two earlier CIA handlers.
Within the cables, Giaka places Megrahi in Malta - where the bomb was said to have been planted - at a key time in the Lockerbie plot.
Megrahi is also said to have visited a Maltese clothes shop, buying shirts and baby grows - which were placed in the suitcase with the bomb and later found at the plane crash site.
Giaka had even talked to the CIA about eight kilos of orange-coloured explosives stored at the Malta airport offices. Semtex, the explosive used in Lockerbie, is orange.
In the 2001 trial, Giaka was to be a "key" witness in the prosecution's case but the four judges described some of his evidence as "at best grossly exaggerated and at worst simply untrue".
The Senussi files
Decades on from Megrahi's conviction, new intelligence documents have been recovered allegedly from the heart of Libyan intelligence.
They are believed to have come from Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi's notorious intelligence network run by his spy chief Abdullah Senussi.
These leaked Libyan intelligence documents contain information that could potentially put an end to the doubt, theories and countertheories that have tied so many, including me, in knots.
The original 'Senussi Files', as they are now known, were shown to French journalists who later published a book, The Murderer Who Must Be Saved.
I travelled to Paris to meet one of the authors, investigative journalist Vincent Nouzille.
He brought piles of documents, enough to cover the whole bed and the hotel room desk.
You can tell he loves his work and despite having pored over these documents for years, he's still awestruck by their content.
Some of the Senussi files date back to autumn 1988, in the months before Lockerbie, and contain documents apparently detailing plans to target aircraft on multi-stop flights using a 11-hour long-delay timer bomb concealed in luggage much like the Lockerbie bombing.
It even mentions tests on concealing a device inside a tape recorder.
As we go through each document, my head is spinning.
There are references to dry runs, apparent weaknesses in airport security, and enough detail about the movements of Megrahi and others for Nouzille to crosscheck dates and places against other sources.
Nouzille says he spent three years carefully verifying everything in the files.
He shows me another file which details the apparent movements of Megrahi and Masud, coming in and out of Malta.
This account lines up with the information provided in the CIA cables from the previously discredited Giaka.
"We know from the CIA cables that Giaka reported the same people, the same dates, the same false passport, at the same date," Nouzille says.
"So two sources, independent, which match."
The Senussi Files seem to corroborate several details first mentioned in the cables, including the presence of semtex at Luqa Airport in Malta.
Nouzille shows me a translated document, signed by Megrahi, dated January 87, which mentions "10 kilos of explosive material" stored at the airport by Lamin Khalif Fhimah, the man who stood trial alongside Megrahi in 2001 but was acquitted.
